chapters.title: Preface
paragraphs: Not only in the world of commerce but also in the world of ideas, our age is staging ein wirklicher Ausverkauf — a real clearance sale. Everything can be had at such a giveaway price that one wonders whether anyone, in the end, will still bother to bid. Every speculative score-keeper who conscientiously marks the meaningful progress of the newer philosophy, every Privatdocent and tutor and student, every outlier and lodger in philosophy, does not stop at doubting everything but goes further. It would perhaps be ill-timed and inopportune to ask them where, exactly, they are going; but it is surely polite and modest to take it as settled that they have indeed doubted everything, since otherwise it would be a strange thing to say that they were going further. This preliminary movement they have, then, all of them performed, and presumably with such ease that they do not find it necessary to drop a single word about how it was done. For not even the man who anxiously and worriedly sought a little enlightenment found any such thing — no guiding hint, no small dietary prescription as to how one is to conduct oneself under this enormous task. ‘But Descartes did it, didn't he?' Descartes, a venerable, humble, honest thinker whose writings surely no one can read without the deepest emotion — he did what he said and said what he did. Alas! alas! alas! that is a great

rarity in our age! Descartes, as he himself often enough repeats, did not doubt with respect to faith. (‘Memores tamen, ut jam dictum est, huic lumini naturali tamdiu tantum esse credendum, quamdiu nihil contrarium a Deo ipso revelatur ..... Præter cætera autem, memoriæ nostræ pro summa regula est infigendum, ea quæ nobis a Deo revelata sunt, ut omnium certissima esse credenda; et quamvis forte lumen rationis, quam maxime clarum et evidens, aliud quid nobis suggerere videretur, soli tamen auctoritati divinæ potius quam proprio nostro judicio fidem esse adhibendam.' Cfr. Principia philosophiæ, pars prima §28 and §76.) He did not cry fire and make it everyone's duty to doubt, for Descartes was a quiet, solitary thinker, not a roaring street-watchman. He modestly confessed that his method had significance only for himself, and that it was grounded in part in his own earlier botched learning. (‘Ne quis igitur putet, me hic traditurum aliquam methodum, quam unusquisque sequi debeat ad recte regendam rationem; illam enim tantum, quam ipsemet secutus sum, exponere decrevi... Sed simul ac illud studiorum curriculum absolvi (sc. juventutis), quo decurso mos est in eruditorum numerum cooptari, plane aliud coepi cogitare. Tot enim me dubiis totque erroribus implicatum esse animadverti, ut omnes discendi conatus nihil aliud mihi profuisse judicarem, quam quod ignorantiam meam magis magisque detexissem.' Cfr. Dissertatio de methodo, pp. 2 and 3.) — What those old Greeks, who also knew a thing or two about philosophy, took to be a task for an entire life, on the grounds that the skill of doubting is not acquired in days and weeks; what the old veteran fighter achieved when he had preserved the equilibrium of doubt through every snare, fearlessly denied the certainty of the senses and the certainty of thought, incorruptibly defied the anxiety of self-love and the insinuations of sympathy — that, in our age, is where everyone *begins*.

In our age, no one stops at faith, but everyone goes further. To ask where they are going might perhaps be foolhardy; but it is surely a sign of breeding and refinement that I assume that everyone has faith, since otherwise it would be a peculiar thing to say that they were going further. In those old days it was different. Then faith was a task for a whole life, because it was assumed that the skill of believing is not acquired in days or weeks. When the seasoned old man drew near his end, having fought the good fight and kept the faith, his heart was still young enough not to have forgotten that fear and trembling which chastened the youth, which the man indeed mastered, but which no human being ever wholly outgrows — except insofar as he should manage, as early as possible, to go further. Where those venerable figures arrived is where, in our age, everyone *begins*, in order to go further.

The present author is by no means a philosopher. He has not understood the System, whether it exists, whether it is finished. He already has enough to do for his weak head with the thought of what an enormous head everyone in our age must have, since everyone has such an enormous thought. Even if one were able to transpose the entire content of faith into the form of the concept, it would not follow from this that one had grasped faith — grasped how one came into it, or how it came into one. The present author is by no means a philosopher; he is, *poetice et eleganter*, a freelance writer who neither writes the System nor writes promises about the System, who neither subscribes himself to the System nor signs himself over to it. He writes because for him it is a luxury that becomes more agreeable and self-evident the fewer there are who buy and read what he writes. He easily foresees his fate in an age that has drawn a line through passion in order to serve science — an age in which an author who wants readers must take care to write in such a way that his book can be conveniently leafed through during the after-dinner nap, and must take care to model his outward appearance after that polite gardener's apprentice in the Adresseavisen who, hat in hand and with good recommendations from the place where he last served, recommends himself to a most honored public. He foresees his fate: to be entirely ignored. He has a presentiment of the still more dreadful prospect that the zealous critic will repeatedly stand him in the corner of the schoolroom; he shudders at the still more dreadful prospect that some industrious registrar, some paragraph-glutton (who, in order to save science, is always ready to do to the writings of others what Trop, ‘to save taste,' magnanimously did to *The Destruction of the Human Race*) will cut him up into §§, and do it with the same inflexibility as the man who, to serve the science of punctuation, divided his speech by counting the words, so that every fifty words made a full stop and every thirty-five a semicolon. — I prostrate myself in the deepest submission before every systematic peeping-Tom: ‘This is not the System; this has not the slightest thing to do with the System. I call down every blessing upon the System and upon the Danish shareholders in this Omnibus — for a tower it will scarcely become. I wish them every one and each of them luck and benediction.'

Most respectfully,
Johannes de Silentio.

chapters.title: Exordium
paragraphs: There was once a man who, as a child, had heard that beautiful tale of how God tested Abraham, and how Abraham endured the temptation, kept the faith, and a second time received a son against all expectation. When he grew older, he read the same story with even greater admiration; for life had separated what had been united in the pious simplicity of the child. The older he grew, the more often his thoughts turned to that tale; his enthusiasm became stronger and stronger, and yet less and less could he understand the story. At last he forgot everything else over it. His soul had only one wish: to see Abraham. One longing: to have been a witness to that event. His desire was not to see the beautiful regions of the East, not the earthly glory of the promised land, not that god-fearing couple whose old age God blessed, not the venerable figure of the aged patriarch, not the vigorous youth of the Isaac whom God had granted — he had no objection to the same thing taking place on a barren heath. His craving was to ride along on those three days when Abraham rode with sorrow before him and Isaac at his side. His wish was to be present in that moment when Abraham lifted his eyes and saw Mount Moriah in the distance, the moment when he left the asses behind and went up the mountain alone with Isaac. For what occupied him was not the artful weaving of the imagination, but the shudder of thought.

That man was no thinker. He felt no urge to go beyond faith. It seemed to him it must be the most glorious thing of all to be remembered as faith's father, an enviable lot to possess it, even if no one knew it.
That man was no learned exegete. He did not know Hebrew. Had he known Hebrew, he would perhaps easily have understood the story of Abraham.
‘And God tested Abraham and said to him: Take Isaac, your only son, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah and offer him there as a burnt offering on a mountain that I will show you.'

It was an early morning. Abraham rose early, had the asses saddled, and left his tent, and Isaac with him. But Sarah looked out the window after them, down through the valley, until she could see them no more. They rode in silence for three days. On the morning of the fourth day Abraham still did not say a word, but lifted his eyes and saw Mount Moriah in the distance. He left the servants behind and went up the mountain alone, leading Isaac by the hand. But Abraham said to himself: ‘I will not hide from Isaac where this journey leads him.' He stood still, he laid his hand on Isaac's head in blessing, and Isaac bent down to receive it. And Abraham's countenance was fatherly, his look was gentle, his speech full of admonition. But Isaac could not understand him; his soul could not be lifted up. He clasped Abraham's knees, he pleaded at his feet, he begged for his young life, for his fair hopes; he reminded him of the joy in Abraham's house, he reminded him of the sorrow and the loneliness. Then Abraham raised the boy up and walked with him hand in hand, and his words were full of comfort and exhortation. But Isaac could not understand him. He climbed Mount Moriah, but Isaac did not understand him. Then he turned away from him for a moment; but when Isaac looked at Abraham's face a second time, it was changed. His look was wild, his figure was terror itself. He seized Isaac by the breast, threw him to the ground, and said: ‘Foolish boy, do you think I am your father? I am an idolater. Do you think this is God's command? No, it is my own desire.' Then Isaac trembled and cried out in his anguish: ‘God in heaven, have mercy on me; God of Abraham, have mercy on me; if I have no father on earth, then be You my father!' But Abraham said softly to himself: ‘Lord in heaven, I thank You; it is better that he believe me to be a monster than that he should lose faith in You.'

When the child is to be weaned, the mother blackens her breast — for it would, after all, be a shame for the breast to look enticing when the child must not have it. So the child believes that the breast has changed; but the mother is the same, her gaze as loving and tender as ever. Blessed is the one who needed no more terrible means to wean the child!

It was an early morning. Abraham rose early, embraced Sarah, the bride of his old age, and Sarah kissed Isaac, who had taken the disgrace from her — her pride, her hope through all generations. So they rode in silence along the road, and Abraham's gaze was fixed on the ground, until on the fourth day, when he lifted his eyes and saw Mount Moriah far off; but his gaze turned again to the ground. In silence he laid the wood in order, in silence he bound Isaac, in silence he drew the knife; then he saw the ram which God had appointed. He sacrificed it and went home. — — — From that day on, Abraham grew old. He could not forget that God had demanded this of him. Isaac thrived as before; but Abraham's eye was darkened, he saw joy no more.

It was an early morning. Abraham rose early. He kissed Sarah, the young mother, and Sarah kissed Isaac, her delight, her joy through all the ages. And Abraham rode along the road deep in thought; he was thinking of Hagar and the son he had driven out into the wilderness. He climbed Mount Moriah, he drew the knife.

It was a quiet evening when Abraham rode out alone, and he rode to Mount Moriah. He cast himself on his face. He prayed God to forgive him his sin — that he had been willing to sacrifice Isaac, that the father had forgotten his duty toward the son. Often he rode that lonely way, but he found no peace. He could not grasp that it was a sin that he had wanted to offer to God the best he possessed, that for which he himself would gladly have given his life many times over; and if it was a sin, if he had not loved Isaac in this way, then he could not understand how it could be forgiven — for what sin was more terrible?

It was an early morning. Everything was prepared in Abraham's house for the journey. He took leave of Sarah, and Eliezer the faithful servant accompanied him along the road, until he turned back again. They rode along together in harmony, Abraham and Isaac, until they came to Mount Moriah. But Abraham prepared everything for the sacrifice, calm and gentle; yet as he turned away and drew the knife, Isaac saw that Abraham's left hand clenched in despair, that a shudder went through his body — but Abraham drew the knife.

Then they returned home, and Sarah hurried to meet them; but Isaac had lost his faith. Not a word about it has ever been said in the world, and Isaac never told a soul what he had seen, and Abraham never suspected that anyone had seen it.
When the child is to be weaned, the mother has the stronger food at hand, that the child may not perish. Blessed is the one who has the stronger food at hand.

In this way and in many similar ways did the man of whom we are speaking think over this event. Each time he returned home from a journey to Mount Moriah, he sank down in weariness, folded his hands, and said: ‘No one was as great as Abraham; who is able to understand him?'

chapters.title: Eulogy on Abraham
paragraphs: If there were no eternal consciousness in a human being, if at the bottom of everything there lay only a wildly fermenting power, twisting in dark passions to bring forth all that was great and all that was insignificant, if a bottomless emptiness, never sated, lay hidden beneath everything — what then would life be but despair? If it were so, if there were no sacred bond uniting humankind, if one generation rose up after another like the leaves of the forest, if one generation succeeded another like the songbirds in the wood, if the human race passed through the world as the ship passes through the sea, as the wind through the desert — a thoughtless and barren labor — if an eternal forgetfulness, always hungry, lay in wait for its prey, and there were no power strong enough to wrest it away from her — how empty and comfortless then would life be! But for that very reason it is not so. And just as God created man and woman, so He fashioned the hero and the poet, or orator. The poet can do nothing of what the hero does; he can only admire him, love him, take joy in him. Yet he too is happy, no less than the hero; for the hero is, as it were, his better self, with whom he is in love, glad that it is not himself, so that his love can be admiration. He is the genius of remembrance, can do nothing but remind us of what has been done, do nothing but admire what has been done. He takes nothing of his own, but is jealous of what has been entrusted to him. He follows the choice of his heart; but once he has found what he sought, he wanders from door to door with his song and his speech, that all may admire the hero as he does, be proud of the hero as he is. This is his deed, his humble work; this is his faithful service in the hero's house. If he remains true to his love in this way, if he struggles day and night with the cunning of forgetfulness, which would steal the hero from him, then he has fulfilled his task; then he is gathered to the hero, who has loved him just as faithfully — for the poet is, as it were, the hero's better self, powerless as a memory is, but transfigured as a memory is. Therefore no one shall be forgotten who was great; and however long it takes, however much the cloud of misunderstanding may carry the hero off, his lover comes nonetheless, and the longer the time has gone on, the more faithfully he clings to him.

No! No one shall be forgotten who was great in the world; but each was great in his own way, and each in proportion to the greatness of what he loved. For he who loved himself became great by himself, and he who loved other human beings became great by his devotion, but he who loved God became greater than all. Each shall be remembered, but each became great in proportion to his expectation. One became great by expecting the possible; another by expecting the eternal; but he who expected the impossible became greater than all. Each shall be remembered, but each was great in proportion to the magnitude of that with which he strove. For he who strove with the world became great by overcoming the world, and he who strove with himself became greater by overcoming himself; but he who strove with God became greater than all. So men strove in the world, man against man, one against

a thousand; but he who strove with God was greater than all. So men strove on the earth: there was one who overcame all by his strength, and there was one who overcame God by his weakness. There was one who relied on himself and won everything; there was one who, secure in his strength, sacrificed everything; but he who trusted in God was greater than all. There was one who was great by his strength, and one who was great by his wisdom, and one who was great by his hope, and one who was great by his love; but Abraham was greater than all — great by that strength whose power is weakness, great by that wisdom whose secret is folly, great by that hope whose form is madness, great by that love which is hatred of self.

By faith Abraham went forth from the land of his fathers and became a stranger in the land of promise. He left one thing behind, took one thing with him: he left his earthly understanding behind, and took faith with him; otherwise he would surely not have set out, but would have thought, this is unreasonable. By faith he was a stranger in the land of promise, and there was nothing to remind him of what was dear to him; on the contrary, everything tempted his soul, by its very newness, to wistful longing. And yet he was the one chosen by God, in whom the Lord was well pleased! Indeed, had he been a cast-off, thrust away from God's grace, he could better have grasped it; as it was, the whole thing seemed like a mockery of him and of his faith. There was, in the world, also one who lived banished from the fatherland that he loved. He is not forgotten, nor are his lamentations, when in his sorrow he sought and found what was lost. From Abraham there is no lamentation. It is human to lament, human to weep with the one who weeps, but it is greater to believe, more blessed to behold the believer. By faith Abraham received the promise that in his seed all the nations of the earth should be blessed. Time passed; the possibility was there; Abraham believed. Time passed; it became unreasonable; Abraham believed. There was one in the world too who had an expectation. Time passed, evening drew on; he was not so wretched as to have forgotten his expectation, and therefore he too shall not be forgotten. Then he grieved, and his grief did not deceive him as life had done; it did for him all that it could; in the sweetness of grief he possessed his disappointed expectation. It is human to grieve, human to grieve with the grieving, but it is greater to believe, more blessed to behold the believer. From Abraham we have no song of mourning. He did not count the days wistfully as the years went by; he did not look at Sarah with suspicious glances, to see whether she was not growing old; he did not stop the course of the sun, that Sarah might not age, and with her his expectation; he did not soothingly sing to Sarah his wistful song. Abraham grew old; Sarah was a mockery in the land — and yet he was God's chosen one and heir to the promise that in his seed all the nations of the earth should be blessed. Then was it not better that he had not been God's chosen? What is it to be God's chosen? Is it to be denied in youth the wish of youth, in order, with great difficulty, to have it fulfilled in old age? But Abraham believed, and held the promise fast. If Abraham had wavered, he would have given it up. He would have said to God: ‘Then perhaps it is not Your will that this should come to pass, so I will give up the wish; it was my only one, it was my blessedness. My soul is sincere, I harbor no secret grudge because You denied it.' He would not have been forgotten — he would have saved many by his example, but he would not have become the father of faith; for it is great to give up one's wish, but it is greater to hold it fast after having given it up; it is great to grasp the eternal, but it is greater to hold fast to the temporal after having given it up. — Then came the fullness of time. Had Abraham not believed, then Sarah would surely have died of grief, and Abraham, dulled by sorrow, would not have understood the fulfillment, but would have smiled at it as at a youthful dream. But Abraham believed, and therefore he was young; for he who always hopes for the best grows old, deceived by life, and he who is always prepared for the worst grows old prematurely; but he who believes preserves an eternal youth. Praised therefore be that story! For Sarah, though stricken in years, was young enough to desire the joy of motherhood, and Abraham, though gray-haired, was young enough to wish to be a father. Outwardly the wonder lies in the fact that it happened in accordance with their expectation; in a deeper sense the wonder of faith lies in the fact that Abraham and Sarah were young enough to wish, and that faith had preserved their wish, and with it their youth. He received the fulfillment of the promise, he received it as a believer, and it came to pass according to the promise and according to the faith — for Moses struck the rock with his staff, but he did not believe.
Then there was joy in Abraham's house, when Sarah stood as bride on the day of her golden wedding.

Yet so it was not to remain. Once again Abraham was to be tried. He had struggled with that cunning power which devises everything, with that vigilant enemy who never sleeps, with that old man who outlives all things — he had struggled with time and kept the faith. Now all the dread of the contest was concentrated into a single moment. ‘And God tested Abraham and said to him: Take Isaac your only son, whom you love, and go to the land of Moriah and offer him there as a burnt offering on a mountain that I will show you.'

So then everything was lost, more dreadful than if it had never come to pass! So the Lord was, after all, only mocking Abraham! Wonderfully He had made the unreasonable real; now He wished to see it annihilated again. It was a folly, but Abraham did not laugh at it, as Sarah had when the promise was first proclaimed. Everything was lost! Seventy years of faithful expectation, the brief joy in faith's

fulfillment. Who then is the one who tears the staff from the old man? Who is the one who demands that he himself shall break it? Who is the one who makes a man's gray hair comfortless? Who is the one who demands that he himself shall do it? Is there no compassion for the venerable old man, none for the innocent child? And yet Abraham was God's chosen one, and it was the Lord who imposed the trial. Was everything now to be lost? The glorious remembrance of the race, the promise in Abraham's seed — was it only a notion, a passing thought the Lord had had, which Abraham must now blot out? That glorious treasure, as old as the faith in Abraham's heart, many many years older than Isaac, the fruit of Abraham's life, sanctified by prayers, ripened in struggles — the blessing on Abraham's lips: was this fruit now to be plucked off untimely and become meaningless? For what meaning had it, when Isaac was to be sacrificed? That wistful but blessed hour, when Abraham was to take leave of all that was dear to him, when he would once more lift up his venerable head, when his face would beam like the Lord's, when he would gather his whole soul into a blessing strong enough to make Isaac blessed all his days — that hour was not to come! For Abraham was indeed to take leave of Isaac, but in such a way that he himself would remain behind; death was to part them, but in such a way that Isaac became its prey. The old man would not lay his blessing hand upon Isaac in joy at the hour of death, but, weary of life, would lay violent hands upon Isaac. And it was God who tested him. Yes, woe! woe to the messenger who came before Abraham with such tidings! Who could have dared to be that envoy of sorrow? But it was God who tested Abraham.

Yet Abraham believed, and believed for this life. Indeed, had his faith been only for a coming life, he might more easily have cast everything aside, in order to hasten out of the world to which he did not belong. But Abraham's faith was not such — if there is such a thing; for properly speaking that is not faith but the most distant possibility of faith, which on the very edge of the horizon catches a glimpse of its object, yet separated from it by a yawning abyss within which despair plays its game. But Abraham believed precisely for this life: that he should grow old in the land, honored among the people, blessed in his lineage, unforgettable in Isaac, the dearest thing in his life, whom he embraced with a love for which it was only a poor expression that he faithfully fulfilled the father's duty of loving the son — as the very wording of the command makes clear: the son whom you love. Jacob had twelve sons and one whom he loved; Abraham had only one, the one he loved.

But Abraham believed, and did not doubt; he believed the unreasonable. Had Abraham doubted — then he would have done something else, something great and glorious; for how could Abraham do other than what is great and glorious? He would have set out for Mount Moriah, he would have split the wood, kindled the fire, drawn the knife — he would have cried out to God: ‘Do not despise this offering; it is not the best that I possess, that I know well; for what is an old man compared with the child of the promise; but it is the best that I can give You. Let Isaac never know of it, that he may comfort himself in his youth.' He would have plunged the knife into his own breast. He would have been admired in the world, and his name would not have been forgotten — but it is one thing to be admired, and another to become a guiding star that saves the anguished.
But Abraham believed. He did not pray for himself, that he might move the Lord; it was only when the just punishment went out over Sodom and Gomorrah that Abraham came forward with his prayers.
We read in those holy Scriptures: ‘And God tested Abraham, and said: Abraham, Abraham, where are you?

And Abraham answered: Here am I.' You, to whom my discourse is addressed, was it so with you? When you saw the heavy dispensations approaching from afar, did you not say to the mountains, hide me, to the hills, fall on me? Or were you stronger — and yet did not your foot drag slowly along the way, did it not long, as it were, to turn back along the old paths? When you were called, did you answer; or did you not answer — perhaps softly, in a whisper? Not so Abraham. Joyfully, freely, confidently, in a loud voice he answered: Here am I. We read further: ‘And Abraham rose early in the morning.' He hastened as though to a feast, and early in the morning he was at the appointed place, on Mount Moriah. He spoke nothing to Sarah, nothing to Eliezer; for who could understand him, and had not the trial, by its very nature, exacted a vow of silence from him? ‘He split the wood, he bound Isaac, he kindled the fire, he drew the knife.' My listener! There has been many a father who believed that in his child he was losing the dearest thing in the world to him, that he was being robbed of every hope of the future; but there was surely no one who, in the same sense as Isaac was for Abraham, was the child of the promise. There has been many a father who lost his child; but then it was God, the Almighty's unchangeable and inscrutable will, His hand that took it. Not so with Abraham. For him a heavier trial was reserved, and Isaac's fate was, with the knife, placed in Abraham's hand. And there he stood, the old man with his only hope! But he did not doubt; he did not look anxiously to the right or the left; he did not challenge heaven with his prayers. He knew it was God the Almighty who was testing him; he knew it was the heaviest sacrifice that could be demanded of him; but he also knew that no sacrifice was too heavy when God demanded it — and he drew the knife.

Who strengthened Abraham's arm, who held his right hand uplifted, that it did not sink down powerless? Whoever looks at this is paralyzed. Who strengthened Abraham's soul, that it did not go black before his eyes, so that he saw neither Isaac nor the ram? Whoever looks at this is blinded. — And yet, perhaps rare is the one who is paralyzed and blinded, rarer still the one who tells worthily what happened. We all know it — it was only a trial.

If Abraham, when he stood on Mount Moriah, had doubted, if he had looked about him in perplexity, if before he drew the knife he had by chance discovered the ram, if God had permitted him to sacrifice it instead of Isaac — then he would have ridden home, everything would have been the same, he had Sarah, he kept Isaac; and yet how changed! For his retreat would have been a flight, his deliverance a chance, his reward shame, his future perhaps perdition. He would then have borne witness neither to his faith nor to God's grace, but only to how dreadful it is to journey up to Mount Moriah. Then Abraham would not have been forgotten, nor Mount Moriah either. But it would have been named not as Ararat, where the ark landed, but as a place of horror, because it was here that Abraham doubted.

Venerable father Abraham! When you went home from Mount Moriah, you needed no eulogy to console you for what was lost; for you won everything and kept Isaac, was it not so? The Lord no longer took him from you, but you sat happily at table with him in your tent, as you do yonder for all eternities. Venerable father Abraham! Millennia have run by since those days, but you need no late-coming lover to wrest your memory from the grip of forgetfulness; for every tongue calls you to mind — and yet you reward your lover more gloriously than anyone, you make him blessed yonder in your

bosom; here you bind his eye and his heart by the wonder of your deed. Venerable father Abraham! Second father of the race! You who first sensed and bore witness to that enormous passion which scorns the dreadful struggle with the raging of the elements and the powers of creation in order to strive with God; you who first knew that highest passion, the holy, pure, humble expression of the divine madness which the heathen admired — forgive him who would speak in your praise, if he did not do it rightly. He spoke humbly, as was the desire of his heart; he spoke briefly, as is fitting; but he shall never forget that you needed a hundred years to receive a son in your old age against all expectation, that you had to draw the knife before you kept Isaac; he shall never forget that in a hundred and thirty years you got no further than to faith.

chapters.title: Preliminary Expectoration
paragraphs: An old proverb, drawn from the outward and visible world, says: ‘Only the one who works gets bread.' Strangely enough, the saying does not apply to the world where it is most at home; for the outward world is subject to the law of imperfection, and here it is repeated again and again that the one who does not work also gets bread, and that the one who sleeps gets it more abundantly than the one who works. In the outward world everything belongs to whoever holds it; this world is enslaved to the law of indifference, and to whoever has the ring, the spirit of the ring obeys, whether he is a Noureddin or an Aladdin; and whoever has the world's treasures has them, no matter how he came by them. In the world of spirit it is otherwise. Here an eternal divine order reigns; here it does not rain on the just and the unjust alike; here the sun does not shine on both the good and the evil. Here it holds true that only the one who works gets bread, only the one who was in anguish finds rest, only the one who descends into the underworld saves the beloved, only the one who draws the knife receives Isaac. He who will not work, he gets no bread, but is deceived as the gods deceived Orpheus with an airy form instead of the beloved — deceived him because he was effeminate, not brave; deceived him because he was a lyre-player, not a man. Here it is no help to have Abraham as one's father, or seventeen ancestors. Of him who will not work, what is written about the virgins of Israel applies: he brings forth wind. But he who will work — he gives birth to his own father.

There is a kind of knowledge that presumes to introduce into the world of spirit the same law of indifference under which the outward world groans. It thinks it is enough to know what is great; no other labor is needed. But for that very reason it does not get the bread; it perishes of hunger while everything turns to gold. And what does it know, anyway? There were many thousands among the Greeks of the time, countless ones in later generations, who knew all the triumphs of Miltiades, but there was only one who lay sleepless over them. There were countless generations who knew the story of Abraham word for word by heart — how many did it make sleepless?

Now the story of Abraham has the remarkable quality that it always remains glorious, however poorly one understands it; but here too the rule holds, that one must be willing to work and to be burdened. But people will not work, and yet they want to understand the story. They speak in praise of Abraham, but how? They give the whole thing a quite ordinary expression: ‘The great thing was that he loved God in such a way that he was willing to sacrifice to him the best he had.' This is very true; but ‘the best' is a vague expression. In the heat of speech and thought one quite blithely identifies Isaac and ‘the best,' and the meditator can comfortably puff at his pipe during the meditation, and the listener can comfortably stretch out his legs. If that rich young man whom Christ met on his way had sold all his goods and given them to the poor, we would praise him as we praise everything that is great, and not even understand him without effort; but he still would not have become an Abraham, even though he sacrificed his best. What people leave out of Abraham's story is the anxiety; for to money I have no ethical obligation, but the father has the highest and holiest obligation toward the son. Yet anxiety is a dangerous matter for the soft-hearted, and so they forget it; and despite this they want to talk about Abraham. So they talk, and in the course of the talk the two expressions ‘Isaac' and ‘the best' alternate; everything goes excellently. But should it happen that there was, among the listeners, a man suffering from sleeplessness, then the most dreadful, the deepest, tragic and comic misunderstanding lies very close at hand. He went home, he wanted to do as Abraham did; for the son is, after all, the best. If that speaker got to know about it, he might perhaps go to him; he would summon up all his clerical dignity and shout: ‘Detestable man, dregs of society — what devil has so possessed you that you would murder your son?' And the priest, who had not noticed any warmth or perspiration when preaching about Abraham, would marvel at himself, at the wrath of seriousness with which he thundered at that poor man; he was pleased with himself, for he had never spoken with such force and unction before. He said to himself and his wife: ‘I am an orator. What was lacking was the occasion; when I preached about Abraham last Sunday I felt nothing of the kind.' If this same orator had a small surplus of understanding to spare, I think he would lose it, if the sinner answered calmly and with dignity: But that is what you yourself preached about last Sunday. How could the priest get such a thing into his head? And yet so it was, and the only fault was that he had not known what he was saying. That there is no poet who could bring himself to prefer such situations to the trifling nonsense with which comedies and novels are filled! The comic and the tragic touch each other here in absolute infinity. The priest's speech was perhaps in itself ridiculous enough, but it became infinitely ridiculous through its effect, and yet that effect was perfectly natural. Or — if the sinner really, without raising any objection, was converted by the priest's chastising sermon, if this zealous cleric went home pleased, pleased in the consciousness that he had effect not only from the pulpit, but above all with irresistible power as pastor of souls — that on Sunday he inspired the congregation, while on Monday like a cherub with flaming sword he placed himself before the man who, by his deed, would put to shame the old saying that things do not go in the world as the priest preaches *.

If, on the other hand, the sinner was not convinced, then his situation is tragic enough. He was then, presumably, executed or sent to the madhouse — in short, he became unhappy in relation to so-called actuality. In another sense, however, I think Abraham made him happy; for the one who works does not perish.

How does one explain a contradiction like that of the speaker just mentioned? Is it because Abraham has acquired a kind of prescriptive right to be a great man, so that what he does is great, and when another does the same it is sin, sin crying to heaven? In that case I have no wish to take part in such thoughtless praise. If faith cannot make it a holy act to be willing to murder one's son, then let the same judgment fall on Abraham as on anyone else. If one perhaps lacks the courage to follow one's thought through, to say that Abraham was a murderer, then it is surely better to acquire that courage than to waste time on undeserved eulogies. The ethical expression for what Abraham did is that he wanted to murder Isaac; the *.

* In the old days they used to say: it is sad that things do not go in the world as the priest preaches — perhaps the time will come, especially with the help of philosophy, when one can say: fortunately, things do not go as the priest preaches; for in life there is at least a little sense, in his sermon there is none at all.

religious expression is that he wanted to sacrifice Isaac; but in this contradiction lies precisely the anxiety that can well make a man sleepless — and yet Abraham is not who he is without this anxiety. Or did Abraham perhaps not do what is told at all? perhaps, given the conditions of those times, it was something quite different — in that case let us forget him; for what is the use of remembering a past that cannot become a present? Or had that speaker perhaps forgotten something, something corresponding to the ethical forgetfulness that Isaac was the son? When faith is taken away by being reduced to nothing and Nichts, then all that remains is the raw fact that Abraham wanted to murder Isaac, which is easy enough for anyone to imitate who does not have faith — that is, the faith that makes it hard for him.

For my own part I do not lack the courage to think a thought through to the end; until now I have feared none. Should I encounter such a one, then I hope I will at least have the honesty to say: this thought I fear, it stirs up something else in me, and so I will not think it. If by this I am doing wrong, then the punishment will not fail to come. If I had recognized as the verdict of truth that Abraham was a murderer, I do not know whether I would have been able to silence my piety toward him. If, however, I had thought it, then I would presumably have kept silent about it, for in such thoughts one should not initiate others. But Abraham is no illusion; he has not slept his way to his renown, he does not owe it to a whim of fate.

Can one then speak unreservedly of Abraham, without running the risk that some individual will go astray and do likewise? If I do not dare to, then I will simply remain silent about Abraham; and above all I will not bring him down so as to make him, by that very act, a snare for the weak. For if one makes faith into everything — that is, into what it is — then I think one can speak of it without danger in our age, which scarcely runs to extravagance in faith; and it is only by faith that one comes to resemble Abraham, not by murder. If one makes love into a fleeting mood, a voluptuous stirring in a person, then one only lays snares for the weak when one wants to talk about love's exploits. Everyone has had a passing emotion; but if therefore everyone wanted to do that dreadful thing which love has hallowed as an immortal exploit, then everything is lost — both the exploit and the deluded one. About Abraham one can well speak; for the great can never harm, when it is grasped in its greatness; it is like a two-edged sword that kills and saves. If the lot fell to me to speak about it, I would begin by showing what a pious and god-fearing man Abraham was, worthy to be called God's chosen one. Only such a man is laid under such a trial; but who is such a man? Next I would describe how Abraham loved Isaac. To this end I would beg all good spirits to stand by me, that my speech might become as glowing as paternal love is. I hope then to depict it in such a way that there would not be many a father in the King's realm and lands who would dare to claim that he loved in this way. But if he did not love as Abraham did, then every thought of sacrificing Isaac would be a temptation. About this one could already speak for several Sundays — there is no need to hurry. The result, if the matter were rightly spoken of, would be that a number of fathers would not at all desire to hear more, but would for now be glad if they really succeeded in loving as Abraham loved. If then there was one who, having heard both the great and the dreadful in Abraham's deed, dared to set out along the way, then I would saddle my horse and ride with him. At every station, until we came to Mount Moriah, I would explain to him that he could still turn back, could still repent the misunderstanding that he was called to be tried in such a struggle, could confess that he lacked the courage, so that God Himself would have to take Isaac, if He wanted him. It is my conviction that such a man is not cast off, that he can become blessed along with all the others, but in time he does not become so. Even in the most believing ages, would one not judge such a man this way? I have known a man who could once have saved my life if he had been magnanimous. He said straight out: ‘I see well enough what I could do; but I dare not, I am afraid that later I shall lack strength, that I shall regret it.' He was not magnanimous; but who would therefore stop loving him?

When I had spoken in this way, when I had moved the listeners so that they had at least sensed the dialectical struggles of faith and its gigantic passion, then I would not be the cause of any error on the part of the listeners, that they should think: ‘Now he has faith to such a high degree, it is enough for us to hold on to his coattails.' I would, namely, add: ‘I have by no means faith. By nature I am a clever head, and every such

head always has great difficulty in making the movement of faith — although I do not, for that, want to ascribe in itself any worth to that difficulty which brought the clever head further by overcoming it than to the point at which the simplest and most
person more easily arrives.'

Yet love has its priests in the poets, and now and then one hears a voice that knows how to keep it in honor; but of faith no word is heard. Who speaks in honor of this passion? Philosophy goes further. Theology sits at the window, made up like a courtesan, and woos its favor, offering its charms for sale to philosophy. It is supposed to be hard to understand Hegel, but to understand Abraham — that is a small matter. To go further than Hegel is a wonder, but to go further than Abraham is the easiest of all. I, for my part, have

spent considerable time on understanding Hegelian philosophy, also believe I have, more or less, understood it, and am bold enough to think that when, in spite of trouble taken, I cannot understand him in certain places, then he himself was probably not entirely clear. All this I do easily, naturally; my head does not suffer for it. But when I have to begin to think about Abraham, I am, as it were, annihilated. At every moment I catch sight of that enormous paradox which is the content of Abraham's life; at every moment I am thrown back, and my thought, despite all its passion, cannot penetrate it, cannot get a hairsbreadth further. I strain every muscle to gain a view of it, and in the same instant I am paralyzed.

I am no stranger to what has been admired in the world as great and magnanimous; my soul feels its kinship with it; in all humility it is convinced that it was my cause too the hero strove for; in the moment of contemplation I cry out to myself: *jam tua res agitur*. I can think myself into the hero; into Abraham I cannot think myself; when I have reached the height, I fall down, since what is offered to me is a paradox. By this I do not mean to say at all that faith is something inferior, but on the contrary, that it is the highest, and that it is dishonest of philosophy to put something else in its place and to make light of faith. Philosophy cannot and shall not give faith, but it shall understand itself and know what it offers, and take nothing away — and least of all swindle people out of something as though it were nothing. I am no stranger to life's troubles and dangers; I do not fear them, and I go to meet them with good cheer. I am not unfamiliar with the dreadful; my memory is a faithful wife, and my imagination is, what I myself am not, an industrious little maid who sits all day quietly at her work, and in the evening knows how to chat so prettily for me that I have to look at it, even though it is not always landscapes or flowers or pastoral idylls she paints. I have looked the dreadful in the eye; I do not flee it in fear; but I know very well that, even though I go to meet it bravely, my courage is not the courage of faith, and not at all to be compared with it. I cannot make the movement of faith; I cannot shut my eyes and confidently plunge into the absurd; for me it is an impossibility, but I do not boast of it. I am convinced that God is love; this thought has for me an original lyrical validity. When it is present to me, I am unspeakably blessed; when it is absent, I long for it more violently than the lover does for the beloved. But I do not believe; this courage I lack. The love of God is, both in the direct and the inverse sense, incommensurable for the whole of actuality. I am not cowardly enough to whine and lament about it for that reason; but neither am I sneaky enough to deny that faith is something far higher. I can well bear to live in my own way; I am glad and content; but my joy is not the joy of faith, and is, compared with that, unhappy. I do not burden God with my little troubles; the particular does not concern me; I gaze only at my love, and keep its virginal flame pure and clear. Faith is convinced that God concerns Himself even with the least. I am content in this life to be married with the left hand; faith is humble enough to demand the right hand — for that it is humility, I do not deny, and shall never deny.

Is it really the case that everyone in my generation is able to make the movements of faith? Unless I have judged it badly, it is rather inclined to be proud of doing what it does not even credit me with being able to do — namely, the imperfect. It goes against my soul to do what so often is done — to speak inhumanly about the great, as if a few thousand years made an enormous distance. I prefer to speak humanly of it, as if it had happened yesterday, and to let only the greatness itself be the distance, which either lifts up or condemns. If I, then (in the capacity of tragic hero — for higher I cannot reach), had been summoned to such an extraordinary royal journey as the one to Mount Moriah, I know well what I would have done. I would not have been cowardly enough to stay home; I would not have lain about loitering on the highway; I would not have forgotten the knife so as to cause a small delay; I am quite certain that I would have been there on the dot, with everything in order — perhaps I would rather have come too early, that it might soon be over. But I also know what I would have done further. The very moment I mounted my horse, I would have said to myself: now everything is lost. God demands Isaac, I sacrifice him, and with him all my joy — yet God is love and continues to be so for me; for in temporal life God and I cannot speak together, we have no language in common. Perhaps someone in our age will be foolish enough, envious enough of greatness, to want to convince himself and me that, if I had really done this, I would have done something even greater than what Abraham did; for my enormous resignation was far more ideal and poetic than Abraham's pettiness. And yet this is the greatest untruth; for my enormous resignation was the *substitute* for faith. I could not, even then, have done more than the infinite movement to find myself and rest again in myself. Nor would I, even then, have loved Isaac as Abraham loved him. That I was resolute enough to make the movement could prove my courage, humanly speaking; that I loved him with my whole soul is the presupposition without which the whole thing becomes a misdeed; but still I would not have loved as Abraham did — for then I would have held back even at the last minute, without therefore arriving too late at Mount Moriah. Furthermore, my conduct would have spoiled the whole story; for if I had got Isaac back, I would have been embarrassed. What was easiest for Abraham would have been hard for me — to be glad in Isaac again! For he who has, with the whole infinity of his soul, *proprio motu et propriis auspiciis*, made the infinite movement and can do no more, keeps Isaac only in pain.

But what did Abraham do? He came neither too early nor too late. He mounted his ass; he rode slowly along the way. All this time he believed; he believed that God would not demand Isaac of him, while he was nevertheless willing to sacrifice him if it was required. He believed by virtue of the absurd; for there could be no question of human calculation, and it was indeed the absurd that God, who demanded this of him, in the next moment was to revoke the demand. He climbed the mountain; even at the moment when the knife flashed, he believed — that God would not demand Isaac. He was indeed taken by surprise at the outcome; but through a double movement he had reached his original state, and therefore he received Isaac more gladly than the first time. Let us go further. Let us suppose Isaac actually was sacrificed. Abraham believed. He did not believe that he should one day be blessed in the hereafter, but that he should be blessed here in the world. God could give him a new Isaac, could call back to life the one sacrificed. He believed by virtue of the absurd; for all human calculation had long since ceased. That sorrow can make a person mentally deranged, that one sees, and it is heavy enough; that there is a force of will that can sail so close to the wind that it saves understanding, even if the person becomes a little odd, that one also sees — I do not mean to belittle it. But to be able to lose one's understanding, and with it the whole of the finite, of which understanding is the broker, and then by virtue of the absurd to win precisely the same finite back — this terrifies my soul; but on that account I do not say that it is something insignificant, for on the contrary, it is the only wonder. People generally think that what faith brings forth is no work of art, that it is coarse and clumsy work, only for the more lumpish natures; yet it is far otherwise. The dialectic of faith is the finest and the most remarkable of all things; it has an elevation of which I can indeed form an idea, but no more. I can make the great trampoline-leap by which I pass over into the infinite; my back is like a tightrope-dancer's, twisted in my childhood, and so it comes easily to me. I can — one, two, three — go head-first into existence; but the next thing I cannot do; for the wondrous I cannot do, I can only marvel at it. Yes, if Abraham, the moment he swung his leg over the ass's back, had said to himself: now Isaac is lost, I might as well sacrifice him here at home as undertake the long journey to Moriah — then I have no need of Abraham, whereas now I bow seven times before his name and seventy times before his deed. This, namely, he did not do; which I can prove from the fact that he was glad to receive Isaac, truly heartily glad — that he needed no preparation, no time to compose himself for finitude and its joy. If it had not been thus with Abraham, then he had perhaps loved God, but not believed; for he who loves God without faith reflects upon himself; he who loves God in faith reflects upon God.

On this peak Abraham stands. The last stage he loses sight of is infinite resignation. He really goes further and arrives at faith; for all those caricatures of faith — the wretched lukewarm sloth that thinks: there is probably no danger, it is not worth grieving before the time; the miserable hope that says: one cannot know what will happen, it is at least possible — these caricatures belong in life's wretchedness, and infinite resignation has already infinitely despised them.

Abraham I cannot understand; in a certain sense I can learn nothing from him without being amazed. If anyone imagines that, by reflecting on the outcome of that story, he should be moved to believe, then he deceives himself, and would cheat God of faith's first movement; he wants to suck life-wisdom out of the paradox. Perhaps it succeeds for one or another, for our age does not stop at faith, at its miracle of turning water into wine — it goes further, it turns wine into water.

Would it not be best, after all, to stop at faith? And is it not outrageous that everyone wants to go further? When in our age — and this is proclaimed in various ways — people will not stop at love, where do they end up? In earthly cleverness, petty calculation, in misery and wretchedness, in everything that can make a person's divine origin doubtful. Would it not be best to stop at faith, and would it not be best for him who stands to take care that he does not fall? For the movement of faith must constantly be made by virtue of the absurd, yet, mark well, in such a way that one does not lose finitude, but wins it whole and entire. For my own part, I can well describe the movements of faith, but I cannot make them. When one wishes to learn to make the swimming movements, one can hang oneself in straps from the ceiling: one describes the movements well enough, but one does not swim. Just so, I can describe the movements of faith; but when I am thrown into the water, I do indeed swim (for I am no waddler), but I make different movements — I make the movements of infinity, while faith does the opposite: after having made the movements of infinity, it makes those of finitude. Blessed is the one who can make these movements; he does the wonderful, and I shall never tire of admiring him, whether it be Abraham or the slave in Abraham's house, whether it be a professor of philosophy or a poor servant girl — it is absolutely indifferent to me; I look only at the movements. But them I do look at, and I will not be fooled, neither by myself nor by any other person. The knights of infinite resignation are easily recognized; their gait is light, daring. Those, on the other hand, who bear the treasure of faith are easily mistaken, because their exterior bears a striking resemblance to what both infinite resignation and faith deeply despise — to philistinism. I confess sincerely, in my practice I have not found a single reliable specimen, although I will not therefore deny that perhaps every other person is such a specimen. Meanwhile I have for several years searched in vain. Generally one travels round the world to see rivers and mountains, new stars, brightly colored birds, deformed fish, ridiculous human races — one gives oneself up to that animal stupor that gapes at existence, and thinks one has seen something. This does not occupy me. If, on the other hand, I knew where such a knight of faith lived, I would travel on foot to him; for this wonder occupies me absolutely. I would not let go of him for a moment; every minute I would watch how he conducted himself in the movements; I would consider myself provided for in life, and divide my time between gazing at him and exercising myself, and so devote all my time to admiring him. As I said, I have not found such a one; meanwhile I can well think him. Here he is. The acquaintance is made; I am introduced to him. The moment I first lay eyes on him, I throw him from me again that very instant, take a leap backward myself, clap my hands together, and say half aloud: ‘Good Lord! is it the man, is it really he? — he looks just like a tax collector!' But still it is he. I draw a little closer to him; I watch the slightest movement, to see whether some little uneven fractional telegraphy from the infinite might not show itself, a glance, a look, a gesture, a touch of melancholy, a smile, that betrayed the infinite by its incongruity with the finite. No! I examine his figure from top to toe, to see whether there might not be some chink through which the infinite peeped out. No! He is solid through and through. His footing? It is firm; it belongs entirely to finitude. No primly dressed burgher walking out to Frederiksberg on a Sunday afternoon treads more solidly on the earth; he belongs entirely to the world; no philistine could belong to it more. None of that strange and superior nature is to be detected, by which one recognizes the knight of the infinite. He delights in everything, takes part in everything, and every time one sees him taking part in a particular thing, it is with the persistence that marks the earthly person whose soul clings fast to such things. He minds his work. When one sees him, one would think he was a clerk who had lost his soul in Italian bookkeeping, so punctual is he. He takes a holiday on Sunday. He goes to church. No heavenly look or sign of the incommensurable betrays him; if one did not know him, it would be impossible to single him out from the rest of the crowd; for his sturdy, vigorous psalm-singing proves at most that he has good lungs. In the afternoon he goes out to the woods. He delights in everything he sees: the throng of people, the new omnibuses, the Sound. When one meets him on the Strandvei, one would think he was some shopkeeper letting himself loose; that is precisely how he enjoys himself, for he is no poet, and I have tried in vain to coax out of him the poetic incommensurability. Toward evening he goes home; his gait is as untiring as a postman's. On the way he thinks that his wife surely has some special little warm dish for him

when he comes home — for example, a roasted lamb's head with vegetables. If he met someone of his own mind, he could go on talking with him about that dish all the way to Østerport with a passion that would befit a restaurateur. As it happens, he has not even four shillings, and yet he believes firmly and steadfastly that his wife has that delicious dish for him. If she has it, then it must be an enviable sight for distinguished people, an inspiring one for the common man, to see him eat; for his appetite is greater than Esau's. His wife does not have it — strangely enough, he is exactly the same. On the way he passes a building site; he meets another man. They talk together for a moment; in an instant he erects a building; he disposes of all the resources for it. The stranger leaves him with the thought: surely that was a capitalist; while my admired knight thinks: well, if it came to that, I could easily get the money. He lies in an open window and looks at the square in which he lives. Everything that goes on — that a rat slips down under a curbstone plank, that the children are at play — everything occupies him with a calm in existence as if he were a sixteen-year-old girl. And yet he is no genius; for the incommensurability of genius I have searched in vain to spy out in him. — He smokes his pipe in the evening hour; when one sees him, one would swear it was the pork-butcher across the way vegetating in the twilight. He lets things slide, with a carefreeness as if he were a frivolous good-for-nothing; and yet every moment he lives, he buys the convenient time at the dearest price, for he does not do the slightest thing except by virtue of the absurd. And yet, yet — yes, I could become furious about it, if for no other reason than envy — yet this person has done and does at every moment the movement of infinity. He drains in infinite resignation the deep melancholy of existence; he knows the blessedness of infinity; he has felt

the pain of renouncing everything, the dearest thing one has in the world; and yet finitude tastes to him just as good as it does to one who never knew anything higher; for his abiding in finitude has no trace of a cowed and anxious training, and yet he has this security to delight in it as if it were the most certain thing of all. And yet, yet, the entire earthly figure he produces is a new creation by virtue of the absurd. He resigned everything infinitely, and then he grasped everything again by virtue of the absurd. He continually makes the movement of infinity, but he does it with such correctness and certainty that he constantly comes out of it with finitude, and there is not a second when one suspects anything else. The most difficult task for a dancer is supposed to be to leap into a definite posture in such a way that there is not a second when he is grasping for the posture, but in the leap itself he stands in the posture. Perhaps no dancer can do it — but this knight does. The mass of people live lost in worldly sorrow and joy; these are the wallflowers, who do not come into the dance. The knights of infinity are dancers and have elevation. They make the movement upward and fall down again, and this too is no unblessed pastime, and not unlovely to look upon. But every time they come down again, they cannot at once assume the pose; they waver a moment, and this wavering shows that, for all that, they are strangers in the world. The wavering is more or less striking, depending on their skill; but even the most skillful of these knights cannot conceal that wavering. One does not need to see them in the air; one need only see them at the moment they touch and have touched the earth — and one knows them. But to be able to come down in such a way that the very second one looks as though one were standing and walking, to transform the leap of life into a walk, to absolutely express the sublime in the pedestrian — that only this knight can do — and this is the only wonder.

Yet this wonder can so easily deceive that I will describe the movements in a particular case which can illuminate their relation to actuality; for it is upon this that everything turns. A young swain falls in love with a princess, and the entire content of his life lies in this love; and yet the relationship is such that it cannot possibly be realized, cannot possibly be translated from ideality into reality *. The slaves of wretchedness, the frogs in life's swamp, naturally cry: such a love is folly; the rich brewer's widow is just as good and solid a match. Let them croak undisturbed in their swamp. The knight of infinite resignation does not do this; he does not give up his love — not for all the glory of the world. He is no fool. He first satisfies himself that this love really is the content of his life, and his soul is too sound and too proud to squander the slightest thing on a binge. He is not cowardly; he does not fear to let it slip into his most secret, his most hidden thoughts, to let it twist itself in countless coils around every ligament of his consciousness — should the love become unhappy, he will then never be able to tear himself away from it. He feels a blessed delight in letting love thrill through every nerve, and yet his soul is solemn as that of one who has drained the cup of poison and feels how the juice penetrates every drop of his blood — for this moment

is life and death. When he has thus drawn the whole of love into himself and become absorbed in it, he does not lack courage to attempt and to risk everything. He surveys the relations of life; he calls together the swift thoughts which, like trained pigeons, obey his every nod; he swings his staff over them, and they hurl themselves in every direction. But when they all return, all of them as messengers of grief, and explain to him that it is an impossibility, then he becomes still; he dismisses them; he is alone — and then he undertakes the movement. If what I am saying here is to have any meaning, it depends on the movement being made *normally* *. The knight will then, first of all, have the strength to concentrate the whole content of life and the meaning of actuality into a single wish. If a person lacks this concentration, this closure — if his soul from the beginning is dispersed in the manifold — then he never comes to make the movement; he will in life act cleverly, like the moneymen who place their capital in many different securities, in order to gain on one when they lose on the other — in short, he is no knight.

* *Ein seliger Sprung in die Ewigkeit.*

The knight will, secondly, have the strength to concentrate the entire result of the operation of thought into a single act of consciousness. If he lacks this closure — if his soul from the beginning is dispersed in the manifold — then he will never have time to make the movement; he will be constantly running errands in life, never entering into eternity. For at the very moment he is closest to it, he will suddenly discover that he has forgotten something, for which he must turn back. In the next moment, he will think, it is possible — and that too is quite true; but by reflections of this kind one never gets to make the movement; with their help one sinks deeper and deeper into the mire.

The knight then makes the movement — but which one? Will he forget the whole thing? — for in this too there is, after all, a kind of concentration. No! For the knight does not contradict himself, and it is a contradiction to forget the entire content of one's life and yet remain the same. He feels no urge to become someone else, and by no means regards it as great. Only the lower natures forget themselves and become something new. So the butterfly has entirely forgotten that it was a caterpillar; perhaps it can in turn so completely forget that it was a butterfly that it can become a fish. The deeper natures never forget themselves and never become anything other than what they were. The knight will then remember everything; but this remembering is precisely the pain, and yet he is, in infinite resignation, reconciled with existence. The love for that princess became for him the expression of an eternal love; it took on a religious character; it transfigured itself into a love for the eternal Being which, while it denied fulfillment, nevertheless reconciled him in the eternal consciousness of its validity in a form of eternity which no actuality can take from him. Fools and young people prattle that everything is possible for a human being. This, however, is a great delusion. Spiritually speaking, everything is possible; but in the world of finitude there is much that is not possible. This impossible the knight makes possible by expressing it spiritually; and spiritually he expresses it by renouncing it. The wish, which would have led him out into actuality but stranded on impossibility, is now bent inward; but it is not for that lost, nor forgotten. Sometimes it is the dim stirrings of the wish in him that awaken the remembrance; sometimes he awakens it himself, for he is too proud to allow that what was the entire content of his life should have been the affair of a fleeting moment. He keeps this love young, and it grows with him in years and in beauty. He needs no occasion in finitude for its growth. From the moment he has made the movement, the princess is lost. He does not need those erotic nerve-tinglings at the sight of the beloved, and so on; nor does he need, in a finite sense, constantly to take leave of her, because in an eternal sense he remembers her, and he knows very well that those lovers who are so eager to see each other once more for a last farewell are right to be so eager, right to think it is the last time — for they will sooner forget each other. He has grasped the deep secret that even in loving another human being one ought to be self-sufficient. He no longer takes any finite account of what the princess does, and precisely this proves that he has made the movement infinitely. Here one can have the opportunity to see whether the movement in the individual is true or feigned. There was the man who also believed that he had made the movement; but lo, time went on, the princess did something else — she married, for example, a prince; then his soul lost the elasticity of resignation. He showed thereby that he had not made the movement rightly; for he who has resigned infinitely is sufficient unto himself. The knight does not annul his resignation; he keeps his love just as young as it was at the first moment; he never lets it slip from him, precisely because he has made the movement infinitely. What the princess does cannot disturb him; it is only the lower natures who have the law for their actions in another person, the premises for their actions outside themselves. If, on the other hand, the princess is of the same mind, then the beautiful will appear. She will then introduce herself into that order of knighthood into which one is not admitted by ballot, but of which everyone is a member who has the courage to introduce himself — that order of knighthood which thereby proves its immortality, that it makes no distinction between man and woman. She too will keep her love young and healthy; she too will have overcome her sorrow, even if she does not, as in the ballad, ‘every night lie at her lord's side.' These two will then in all eternity belong together, with such a metrically harmonious *harmonia praestabilita* that, if ever the moment came — a moment that, however, does not finitely occupy them, for then they grow old — if ever the moment came that allowed the love to express itself in time, then they would be able to begin precisely where they would have begun, if they had originally been united. He who understands this, whether man or woman, can never be deceived; for it is only the lower natures who imagine that they are deceived. No girl who is not so proud truly understands how to love; but if she is so proud, then all the cunning and craft of the world cannot deceive her.

In infinite resignation there is peace and rest; every person who wills it, who has not debased himself by — what is even more dreadful than being too proud — looking down on himself, can train himself to make this movement, which in its pain reconciles one with existence. Infinite resignation is that shirt of which the old folktale speaks. The thread is spun in tears, bleached in tears, the shirt sewn in tears; but then it also protects better than iron and steel. The flaw in the folktale is that a third party can prepare this linen. The secret of life is that each must sew it for himself, and the remarkable thing is that a man can sew it just as well as a woman. In infinite resignation there is peace and rest and consolation in pain — that is, when the movement is made normally. It would not, however, have been hard for me to write a whole book if I were to go through all the misunderstandings, the back-to-front postures, the slovenly movements that I have come across in my own little practice. People believe very little in spirit; and yet it is precisely on spirit that this movement depends. It is essential that it not be the one-sided result of a *dira necessitas*; and the more this is present, the more doubtful it always becomes whether the movement is normal. So when one wants to maintain that cold, sterile necessity necessarily must be present, one is saying that no one can experience death before he actually dies — which seems to me a crass materialism. But in our age people are less concerned with making clean movements. If someone learning to dance were to say: now for centuries one generation after another has learned the positions, it is high time I made use of this and went straight to the quadrilles, then one would surely laugh a little at him. But in the world of spirit one finds it eminently plausible. What then is education? I thought it was the course an individual ran in order to catch up with himself; and the one who will not go through this course is helped very little by being born in the most enlightened age.

Infinite resignation is the last stage that precedes faith, so that anyone who has not made this movement does not have faith; for it is only in infinite resignation that I become clear to myself in my eternal validity, and only then can there be any question of grasping existence by virtue of faith.

We will now let the knight of faith make his appearance in the case under discussion. He does exactly the same as the other knight: he renounces infinitely the love that is the content of his life; he is reconciled in pain. But then the wonder happens: he makes one more movement, more wondrous than all, for he says: I nevertheless believe that I shall get her — by virtue, that is, of the absurd, by virtue of the fact that for God all things are possible. The absurd does not belong to the differences that lie within the compass of understanding itself. It is not identical with the improbable, the unexpected, the unforeseen. The moment the knight resigned, he satisfied himself of the impossibility, humanly speaking; that was the result of the understanding, and he had energy enough to think it. In the infinite sense, however, it was possible — that is, by resigning it; but this possessing is at the same time a giving up; yet still this possessing is, for the understanding, no absurdity, for the understanding continued to be right, that in the world of wretchedness over which it rules, it was and remained an impossibility. The knight of faith has this consciousness just as clearly. The only thing that can save him, then, is the absurd, and this he grasps by faith. He acknowledges, therefore, the impossibility, and in the same moment he believes the absurd; for if, without acknowledging the impossibility with the full passion of his soul and with all his heart, he wants to imagine he has faith, he deceives himself, and his testimony has no place anywhere, since he has not even arrived at infinite resignation.

Faith, therefore, is no aesthetic emotion, but something far higher, precisely because it has resignation behind it; it is not the immediate impulse of the heart, but the paradox of existence. So when a young girl, in spite of all difficulties, holds firm to the conviction that her wish will surely be fulfilled, this conviction is by no means the conviction of faith — even though she has been brought up by Christian parents, and may have spent a whole year being instructed by the priest. She is convinced in all her childlike naïveté and innocence; this conviction too ennobles her being and gives her a supernatural stature, so that she can, like a wonder-worker, exorcise the finite forces of existence and bring even stones to weep, while on the other hand, in her flutter, she can just as well run to Herod as to Pilate, and move all the world with her prayers. Her conviction is most lovable, and one can learn much from her; but one thing one does not learn from her: one does not learn how to make the movements; for her conviction does not dare, in the pain of resignation, to look impossibility in the eye.

That it requires strength and energy and freedom of spirit to make the infinite movement of resignation — this I can well perceive; I can also perceive that it can be done. The next thing astonishes me; my brain reels in my head; for, after having made the movement of resignation, then by virtue of the absurd to receive everything, to receive the wish whole and undiminished — that is beyond human powers, that is a wonder. But this much I can perceive: that the young girl's conviction is mere frivolity in comparison with the unshakability of faith, although faith has perceived the impossibility. Every time I want to make this movement, it goes black before my eyes; in the same instant I admire it absolutely, and in the same instant a tremendous anxiety seizes my soul, for what then is it to tempt God? And yet this movement is faith's, and remains so, even if philosophy, in order to confuse the concepts, would have us believe that it has faith, even if theology will sell it off cheap.

To resign requires no faith; for what I gain in resignation is my eternal consciousness, and this is a purely philosophical movement, which I trust myself to make whenever it is required, and which I can train myself to make. For every time some finitude wants to grow over my head, I starve myself out until I make the movement; for my eternal consciousness is my love for God, and that is higher to me than everything else. To resign requires no faith; but to receive the very least more than my eternal consciousness requires faith, for this is the paradox. People often confuse the movements. They say that one needs faith in order to renounce everything; indeed, one hears something even stranger — that a person complains that he has lost his faith, and when one looks at the scale to see where he is, one sees, oddly enough, that he has only reached the point at which he is to make the infinite movement of resignation. By resignation I renounce everything; this movement I make by myself, and when I do not make it, it is because I am cowardly and soft and without enthusiasm, and do not feel the meaning of the high dignity to which every human being is appointed: to be his own censor — which is far more distinguished than being censor general for the whole Roman republic. This movement I make by myself, and what I gain by it is myself in my eternal consciousness, in blessed agreement with my love for the eternal Being. By faith I renounce nothing; on the contrary, by faith I receive everything, precisely in the sense in which it is said that he who has faith like a mustard seed can move mountains.
