If he does this, then the tragic hero is the beloved son of ethics, in whom she is well pleased. If he is silent, it may be because he thereby believes he is making it easier for others; but it may also be because he is making it easier for himself by it. Yet this he knows himself to be free of. If he is silent, then he as the single individual takes upon himself a responsibility, insofar as he overlooks an argument that may come from outside. This he as a tragic hero cannot do; for ethics loves him for that very reason, that he constantly expresses the universal. His heroic deed demands courage, but to this courage belongs also that he does not withdraw from any argumentation. Now it is certain that tears are a dreadful *argumentum ad hominem*, and there has surely been the man who was moved by nothing yet was moved by tears. In the play, Iphigenia gets leave to weep; in actuality there should be granted to her, as to Jephthah's daughter, two months in which to weep, not in solitude, but at her father's feet, and to use all her art, ‘which is only tears,' and to wind herself like an olive branch about his knees (cf. v. 1224).
Aesthetics demanded disclosure but helped itself out with an accident; ethics demanded disclosure, and found in the tragic hero its satisfaction.

In spite of the strictness with which ethics demands disclosure, it cannot be denied that secrecy and silence really make a person great, precisely because they are determinations of inwardness. When Amor leaves Psyche, he says to her: you shall bear a child, who shall be a divine child, if you are silent, but a human one, if you betray the secret. The tragic hero, who is ethics' favorite, is the pure human being; him I can also understand, and all his enterprise too is in the open. If I go further, then I constantly run up against the paradox, the divine and the demonic; for silence is both. Silence is the demon's snare; and the more one is silent, the more dreadful the demon becomes; but silence is also the deity's communion with the single individual,

before I, however, pass over to the story of Abraham, I will call forth a couple of poetic individualities. By the power of dialectics I keep them on the peak, and as I swing the discipline of despair over them, I shall surely keep them from standing still,

that, if possible, in their anxiety they may discover one or another thing *. Aristotle relates in his *Politics* a story of a political disturbance in Delphi, which had its ground in a marriage affair. The bridegroom, to whom the augurs predict a misfortune that will have its origin in his marriage, suddenly changes his plan in the decisive moment, when he comes to fetch the bride — he will not hold the wedding. I need no more. In Delphi this

These movements and postures may still become the object of aesthetic treatment; whether, however, faith and the whole life of faith can become so, I leave here undecided. I will only — because it is always a joy to me to thank the one to whom I owe something — thank Lessing for the few hints about a Christian drama that are found in his *Hamburgische Dramaturgie*. He has, however, fixed his gaze on the purely divine side of this life (the consummated victory), and therefore he has despaired; perhaps he would have judged otherwise had he paid more attention to the purely human side. (*Theologia viatorum*.) What he says is unmistakably very brief, in part evasive; but since I am always very glad when I can have an opportunity to bring Lessing in, I bring him in straightaway. Lessing was not only one of the most comprehensive heads Germany has owned; he was not only in possession of a quite rare promptness in his knowledge — which makes one able to rely securely on him and his autopsy without fearing being deceived by loose citations that have no place anywhere, half-understood phrases drawn from unreliable handbooks, or being disoriented by some stupid trumpeting of novelties which the older writers had set forth far better — he had besides a most uncommon gift for explaining what he himself had understood. There he stopped; in our age, people go further, and explain more than they themselves have understood.

event scarcely went off without tears; if a poet wished to adopt it, he could surely count on sympathy. Is it not dreadful, that love, which often enough has been an exile in life, is now also robbed of heaven's assistance? Is the old saying that marriage is established in heaven not put to shame here? Otherwise it is all the troubles and difficulties of finitude that, like evil spirits, would separate the lovers, while love has heaven on its side, and therefore this holy alliance conquers all enemies. Here it is heaven itself that separates what heaven itself has, after all, joined together. Who would have suspected this? Least of all, surely, the young bride. Only a moment ago she sat in her room in all her beauty, and the lovely girls had conscientiously decked her out so that they could answer for it before all the world, so that they had not only joy of it but envy — yes, joy that it was impossible for them to be more envious, because it was impossible for her to be more beautiful. She sat alone in her room, and was transformed from beauty to beauty; for everything that womanly art could achieve was used to deck out the worthy worthily; but there was still something lacking which the young girls had not dreamed of: a veil finer, lighter, and yet more concealing than that in which the young girls had wrapped her — a bridal robe of which no young girl knew, or could be of help in. The historical catastrophe was, according to Aristotle, the following: in order to revenge themselves, the family slip a temple-vessel in among his household goods, and he is condemned as a temple-

robber. This, however, is a matter of indifference; for the question is not whether the family is clever or stupid in taking revenge — the family acquires only ideal significance insofar as it is drawn into the hero's dialectic. It is, moreover, fateful enough that he, in trying to escape the danger by not marrying, plunges into it, and that his life in a double way comes into contact with the divine — first by the augur's saying, then by being condemned as a temple-robber. \[The bride was not even able to help herself.\] It was an invisible, friendly power that delights in adorning a bride that wrapped her in it, without her knowing anything of it; for she only saw the bridegroom go past and go up to the temple. She saw the door close behind him, and she became still calmer and more blissful; for she knew that he now belonged to her more than ever. The temple's door opened; he stepped out; but she lowered her eye in maidenly fashion, and so she did not see that his face was confused; but he saw that heaven was indeed envious of the bride's loveliness and his happiness. The temple's door opened; the young girls saw the bridegroom step out; but they did not see that his face was confused, for they were busy fetching the bride. Then she stepped forth in all her maidenly humility and yet as a sovereign, surrounded by her train of young girls, who curtsied to her, as the young girl always curtsies to a bride. So she stood at the head of the lovely company, and waited — it was only a moment, for the temple was right there — and the bridegroom came — but he passed by her door.

But I break off here; I am no poet, and only proceed dialectically. The first thing to note is that it is in the decisive moment that the hero gets that revelation; he is then pure and without remorse, has not frivolously bound himself to the beloved. Next, he has a divine pronouncement for him, or rather against him; he is then not, like those slender lovers and beloveds, governed by self-cleverness. It follows further as a matter of course that this pronouncement makes him just as unhappy as the bride — yes, a little more so, since he is, after all, the occasion. For while it is true that the augurs predicted only a misfortune to him, the question is whether this misfortune is not of such a kind that, in striking him, it will also strike their married happiness. What is he now to do? 1) Shall he be silent and hold the wedding, and think: misfortune perhaps does not come at once; in any case I have asserted my love and not feared to make myself unhappy; but be silent I must, or else even the brief moment is forfeited. This seems plausible, but it is by no means so; for in that case he has wronged the girl. He has by his silence in a way made the girl guilty; for if she had known of it, she surely would never have given her consent to such a union. He will then in the time of need have not only the misfortune to bear, but also the responsibility that he was silent — her just anger that he was silent. 2) Shall he be silent and refrain from holding the wedding? In that case he must enter upon a mystification by which he annihilates himself in his relation to her. This perhaps aesthetics would approve. The catastrophe could then be shaped after the manner of the actual one, only that in the last moment it would come to an explanation, which would, however, be after the fact, since aesthetically considered it becomes a necessity to let him die — unless this science should see itself able to lift that ill-omened prophecy. In the meantime this conduct, however magnanimous it may be, contains a wrong against the girl and the actuality of her love. 3) Shall he speak? One must of course not forget that our hero is a little too poetic for renouncing his love to have for him any other meaning than a failed business speculation. If he speaks, then the whole thing becomes an unhappy love story in the same style as Axel and Valborg *. They become a pair whom heaven itself

* Moreover, from this point one could enter another direction of dialectical movements. Heaven predicts a misfortune to him from his marriage, so he could refrain from holding the wedding, but for that reason not give up the girl, but live in a romantic union with her, which for the lovers was more than securing. This, however, contains a wrong against the girl, because in his love for her he does not express the universal.

The very difficult thing about the dialectic in this matter is that the misfortune is to strike only him. They do not get, as Axel and Valborg do, a common expression for their suffering, while heaven equally separates Axel and Valborg, because they are equally near each other. If this were the case here, then a way out could be conceived. For since heaven uses no visible power to separate them, but leaves it to themselves, then it could be conceived that they resolved together to defy heaven and its misfortune.
Ethics, however, will demand of him that he

In the meantime it would be a task both for a poet and for an ethicist who would defend marriage. In general, poetry, when it becomes attentive to the religious and to the inwardness of individuality, would acquire far more meaningful tasks than those with which it now busies itself. Again and again one hears in poetry this story: a man is bound to one girl whom he once loved, or perhaps never really loved, for now he has seen another girl who is the ideal. A man takes a wrong turn in life: the street was right, but it was the wrong house, for across the way on the third floor lives the ideal — that is what people think is a task for poetry. A lover has been mistaken; he has seen the beloved by candlelight and thought she had dark hair, but lo! on closer inspection she had blond — but the sister, that is the ideal. That is what people think is a task for poetry. My opinion is that every such man is a Laban who can be insufferable enough in life, but who should be hooted off the stage at once when he wants to make himself important in poetry. Only passion against passion gives a poetic collision, not this rummaging among trivialities within the same passion. When a girl, for example, in the Middle Ages, after having fallen in love, becomes convinced that earthly love is a sin and prefers a heavenly one, then there is a poetic collision, and the girl is poetic; for her life is in the idea.

His heroism essentially comes to consist in this: that he gives up the aesthetic magnanimity which, *in casu*, could not easily be thought to have any tincture of that vanity that lies in being hidden, since it must, after all, be clear to him that he nevertheless makes the girl unhappy. The actuality of this heroism, however, depends on its having had and having lifted its presupposition; for otherwise one could, especially in our age, get heroes enough — in our age, which has driven it to a matchless virtuosity in the forgery that makes the highest into a matter of skipping over the intermediary.

But to what end now this sketch, since after all I do not get further than to the tragic hero? Because it was, after all, possible that it might cast a light upon the paradox. Everything depends, then, on what relation he stands in to the augur's pronouncement, which in one way or another becomes decisive for his life. Is this pronouncement *publici juris* or is it a *privatissimum*? The scene is in Greece; an augur's pronouncement is intelligible to all — I do not mean only that the single individual can lexically understand the content, but that the single individual can understand that an augur announces to the single individual the decision of heaven. The augur's pronouncement is then intelligible not only to the hero, but to all, and there results no private relation to the deity from it. He can do whatever he will; what is foreshadowed will happen, and he comes neither by doing nor by leaving undone into a closer relation to the deity, becomes neither the object of its grace nor of its wrath. The outcome every single individual will be able to understand just as well as the hero, and there is no secret writing which only the hero can read. Insofar as he then wishes to speak, he can do so excellently, for he can make himself understandable; insofar as he wishes to be silent, it is because, by virtue of being the single individual, he wants to be higher than the universal — wants to dazzle himself with all sorts of fantastic notions about how she will soon forget the matter, and so on.

If, on the other hand, heaven's will had not been proclaimed to him by an augur, if it had come to his knowledge altogether privately, if it had set itself in an entirely private relation to him — then we are at the paradox, if it otherwise exists (for my consideration is dilemmatic); for then he could not speak, however gladly he would. He did not then enjoy himself in the silence, but he suffered the pain; but this very pain was for him the assurance that he was justified. His silence had then its ground not in his wishing as the single individual to set himself in an absolute relation to the universal, but in his being as the single individual placed in an absolute relation to the absolute. He would also be able to find rest in this, as I can imagine, while his magnanimous silence would constantly be disturbed by the demands of the ethical. It would, in general, be desirable if aesthetics one day would try to begin where, for so many years, it has ended — namely, with the illusory magnanimity. As soon as it did this, it would work right into the hands of the religious; for this power is the only one that can save the aesthetic out of its struggle with the ethical. Queen Elizabeth sacrificed her love for Essex to the state by signing his death warrant. This was a heroic deed, even if there was a little personal offense involved — that he had not sent her the ring. As is well known, he had done so, but by the malice of a lady-in-waiting it had been held back. Elizabeth received, so it is told *ni fallor*, the news of this; thereupon she sat for ten days with one finger in her mouth, biting it without saying a single word, and then she died. This was a task for a poet who knew how to wrench her mouth open; otherwise it is at most usable for a ballet master, with whom the poet in our age often enough confuses himself.

Now I will let a sketch follow in the direction of the demonic. For this I can use the legend of Agnes and the Merman. The merman is a seducer who shoots up out of the abyss's hiding-place, and in wild lust seizes and breaks the innocent flower that, in all its grace, stood at the seashore and pensively bent its head at the murmuring of the sea. This has so far been the poets' view. Let us make a change. The merman was a seducer. He has called Agnes; by his ingratiating speech he has lured forth the hidden in her; she has found in the merman what she sought, what she gazed after down at the bottom of the sea. Agnes wants to follow him. The merman has placed her on his arm; Agnes flings her arms about his neck; she gives herself trustingly with her whole soul to the stronger one. He stands already at the shore; he leans out over the sea to plunge down with his prey — then Agnes looks at him once more, not fearfully, not doubting, not proud of her happiness, not intoxicated with lust, but absolutely believing, but absolutely humble as the lowly flower she thought herself to be; absolutely trustingly she entrusts her whole fate to him with this glance. — And see! The sea no longer roars, its wild voice falls silent, the passion of nature, which is the merman's strength, leaves him in the lurch; it becomes a dead calm — and still Agnes looks at him in that way. Then the merman collapses; he cannot withstand the power of innocence; his element becomes faithless to him; he cannot seduce Agnes. He leads her home again; he explains to her that he only wanted to show her how beautiful the sea is when it is still, and Agnes believes him. — Then he turns back alone, and the sea storms; but the despair in the merman storms more wildly. He can seduce Agnes; he can seduce a hundred Agneses; he can charm any girl — but Agnes has won, and the merman has lost her. Only as prey can she become his; faithfully he can belong to no girl, for he is, after all, only a merman. I have allowed myself a small alteration * with the merman; basically I have also altered Agnes a little, for in the legend Agnes is not entirely without guilt, just as it is, in general, nonsense and flirtation and an offense against the female sex to imagine a seduction in which the girl has no, no, no guilt at all. Agnes, in the legend — to modernize my expression a little — is a woman who demands the interesting; and any such girl can always be sure that there is a merman

It is therefore very stupid, or else it is a rumor that some merman has had circulated, that so-called education protects a girl against seduction. We will now give the merman a human consciousness, and let his being a merman signify a human pre-existence, in whose consequence his life was entangled. There is nothing to prevent him from becoming a hero, for the step he now takes is reconciling. He is saved by Agnes; the seducer is crushed; he has bowed under the power of innocence; he can never again seduce. But in the same instant two powers contend over him: repentance, and Agnes and repentance. If repentance takes him alone, then he is hidden; if Agnes and repentance take him, then he is manifest.

Insofar now as repentance takes hold of the merman and he remains hidden, then he has indeed made Agnes unhappy; for Agnes loved him in all her innocence; she believed it was true that, in that moment when he appeared changed even to her, however well he hid it, he only wanted to show her the beautiful stillness of the sea. The merman, however, even in respect to passion, becomes still more unhappy; for he loved Agnes with a multiplicity of passions, and besides has a new guilt to bear. The demonic in repentance will now indeed explain to him that this is precisely his punishment, and the more it tortures him the better.

If he gives himself up to this demonic, then he perhaps makes one more attempt to save Agnes — in the way that, in a certain sense, one can save a person by means of evil. He knows that Agnes loves him. Could he wrest from Agnes this love, then she would, in a way, be saved. But how? To count on this, that an open-hearted confession should awaken her revulsion — for that the merman is too clever. He will then perhaps see fit to inflame all dark passions in her, scorn her, mock her, make her love into a laughing-stock, if possible egg on her pride. He will not spare himself any torment, for this is the deep contradiction in the demonic; and there dwells, in a certain sense, infinitely more good in a demonic person than in trivial people. The more selfish Agnes is, the more easily will she be deceived (for it is only very inexperienced people who think it easy to deceive innocence; existence is most profound, and it is the easiest thing for the wise to dupe the wise) — but the more dreadful will the merman's sufferings be. The more cunningly his deception is laid, the less will Agnes bashfully hide her suffering from him; she will use every means, which then will not be without effect — that is, not to shake him, but to torment him.

By means of the demonic the merman would, then, be the single individual who as the single individual was higher than the universal. The demonic has the same property as the divine: that the single individual can enter into an absolute relation to it. This is the analogy, the counterpart, to the paradox of which we are speaking. It has therefore a certain similarity, which can deceive. Thus the merman has apparently the proof that his silence is justified, in that he in it suffers all his pain. Meanwhile there is no doubt that he can speak. A tragic hero he can become, in my view a grandiose tragic hero, if he speaks. Few perhaps will only grasp wherein the grandiose lies *. Aesthetics at times treats something similar with its usual flirtatiousness. The merman is saved by Agnes, and the whole thing ends with a happy marriage. A happy marriage! that is easy enough. \[He will have\] courage to wrest from himself every self-deception that he could make Agnes happy by his art; he will have courage, humanly speaking, to crush Agnes. By the way, I will here only make a psychological remark. The more selfishly Agnes has been developed, the more dazzling will the self-deception be; indeed, it is not unthinkable that it could happen in actuality that a merman, by his demonic shrewdness, humanly speaking, not only had saved an Agnes but had brought something extraordinary out of an Agnes; for a demon knows how to torture forces out of even the weakest person, and he can, in his own way, mean very well by a person. The merman stands on a dialectical peak. If he is saved out of the demonic in repentance, then there are two ways possible. He can hold himself back, remain in the hidden, but not rely on his shrewdness. He does not then come, as the single individual, into an absolute relation to the demonic, but finds rest in the counter-paradox that the deity will save Agnes. (So the Middle Ages, surely, would make the movement; for the merman is, evidently, according to its concept, due to enter the cloister.) Or he can be saved by Agnes. This must now not be understood as if by Agnes's love he should be saved from becoming a seducer in the future (this is an aesthetic attempt at rescue, which always passes by the main thing — namely, the continuity of the merman's life); for in this respect he is saved; he is saved insofar as he becomes manifest. He then marries Agnes. In the meantime he must take refuge in the paradox. For when the single individual has, by his guilt, come outside the universal, then he can return to it only by virtue of being, as the single individual, in an absolute relation to the absolute. Here I will now make a remark by which I say more than has been said at any point in the foregoing **. Sin is not the first immediacy; sin is a later immediacy. In sin the single individual is already, in the direction of the demonic paradox, higher than the universal, because it is a contradiction of the universal to want to demand itself of the one who lacks the *conditio sine qua non*. If philosophy, among other things, also gave thought to the fact that it might occur to a person to want to act according to its teachings, then one would get a strange comedy out of it. An ethic that ignores sin is a perfectly idle science; but if it makes sin valid, then it is *eo ipso* beyond itself. Philosophy teaches that the immediate shall be annulled. This is true enough; but what is not true is that sin is, without further ado, the immediate, just as little as faith is, without further ado, the immediate. — A happy marriage! it is easy enough. If, on the other hand, ethics is to give the speech at the wedding, then I think it will be another matter. Aesthetics throws the cloak of love over the merman, and then everything is forgotten. It is also careless enough to think that it goes with a marriage as at an auction, where everything is sold in the condition in which it is found at the moment of the hammer-blow. It only sees to it that the lovers get each other; the rest it does not bother itself about. If it would only see what happens afterwards — but for that it has no time; it is at once in full swing clapping a new loving pair together. Aesthetics is the most faithless of all the sciences. The analogy to Abraham, then, will only show itself after the single individual is brought to the point of being able to do the universal, and now the paradox is repeated. The merman's movements I can therefore understand, while I cannot understand Abraham; for the merman comes precisely through the paradox to want to realize the universal. For if he remains hidden and gives himself up to all the torments of repentance, then he becomes a demon, and as such is annihilated. If he remains hidden, but does not think shrewdly that by being himself tormented in the bondage of repentance he can work Agnes loose, then he gets peace, but he is lost to this world. If he becomes manifest, lets himself be saved by Agnes, then he is the greatest human being I can imagine; for it is only aesthetics that frivolously thinks to praise the power of love by letting the lost one be loved by an innocent girl and thereby saved; it is only aesthetics that sees wrongly, and believes that the girl is the heroine, instead of that the merman is. The merman cannot, then, belong to Agnes without his having, after making the infinite movement of repentance, made one more movement — the movement by virtue of the absurd. By his own strength he can make the movement of repentance; but he uses absolutely all his strength on it, and therefore he cannot, by his own strength, come back and grasp actuality. When one has not passion enough to make either the one or the other movement, when one slouches through life, repents a bit and thinks: the rest will go by itself — then one has, once and for all, renounced living in the idea, and then one can very easily attain, and help others attain, the highest, i.e., dazzle oneself and others into the notion that in the world of spirit it goes as in a game of *gnav*, where everything goes any which way. One can then amuse oneself by considering how strange it is that, precisely in an age when everyone, after all, can do the highest, doubt about the immortality of the soul can be so widespread; for he who has really made even the movement of infinity scarcely doubts. The conclusions of passion are the only reliable ones, i.e., the only convincing ones. Fortunately existence is here more loving, more faithful, than what wise men maintain; for it excludes no person, not even the lowliest; it cheats no one, for in the world of spirit only the one who cheats himself is cheated. It is the opinion of all, and insofar as I dare allow myself to judge of this, it is also my opinion, that it is not the highest to enter a cloister; but this is by no means therefore my opinion that in our age, when no one enters a cloister, everyone is greater than the deep and serious souls who found rest in a cloister. How many in our age have passion enough to think it, and then to judge themselves honestly? The mere notion of taking time so upon one's conscience, of giving it time in its sleepless tirelessness to investigate every secret thought, in such a way that, if one does not at every moment make the movement by virtue of the noblest and holiest in a person, one can, with anxiety and dread, discover *, and if by nothing else, then by anxiety lure forth the dim stirring which still hides itself in every human life — while, when one lives in society with others, one so easily forgets, so easily lets go of it, is held up in so many ways, gets the chance to begin afresh —

This people do not believe in our serious age, and yet it is remarkable enough that even in the, by its essence, more frivolous and less thoroughly reflected paganism, the two real representatives of the Greek view of existence — *gnothi seauton* — each in his own way have hinted that, by sinking into oneself, one first and foremost discovers the disposition to evil. this notion alone, grasped with proper reverence, I thought might chastise many an individual in our age, who already thinks himself to have come to the highest. Yet about this people in our age — who have come to the highest — concern themselves little, while no age, like precisely this one, has been forfeit to the comic. And it is incomprehensible that it has not already happened that the age itself, by a *generatio aequivoca*, has spawned its hero, the demon, who relentlessly will perform the dreadful drama: to make the whole age laugh, and to make it forget that it laughs at itself. Or what is existence worth more than to be laughed at, when one has already in one's twentieth year come to the highest? And yet what higher movement has the age devised since the time when people gave up entering the cloister? Is it not a wretched life-wisdom, cleverness, faintheartedness, that sits in the high seat, that cowardly tells people they have done the highest, and slyly keeps them from even attempting the lesser? He who has made the cloister-movement has only one movement left, the movement of the absurd. How many in our age understand what the absurd is? How many in our age live in such a way that they have given up everything, or have got everything? How many are even so honest that they know what they can and what they cannot? And is it not true, that insofar as one finds such people, one finds them most readily among the less educated and partly among women? The age reveals — as a demonic person always reveals himself without understanding himself — its defect in a kind of clairvoyance; for it demands again and again the comic. Should it really be that, that the age needs? Should the theater perhaps need a new play in which it would be made ridiculous that someone died of love? Or would it not rather be saving for the age, if it happened among us, if the age became witness to such an event — that it might at last get the courage to believe in the power of spirit, the courage not, cowardly, to stifle the better in oneself, enviously to stifle it in others — by laughter? Should the age really need a ridiculous *Erscheinung* of one awakened, in order to get something to laugh at; or would it not rather need that such an inspired figure remind it of what was forgotten?

If one wanted a sketch in a similar style, which would, however, because the passion of repentance was not set in motion, become more touching, then one could use for it a story that occurs in the Book of Tobit. The young Tobias wishes to marry Sarah, the daughter of Raguel and Edna. With this girl there is a sad business. She has been given to seven men, all of whom have perished in the bridal chamber. This is, with respect to my sketch, a blemish in the story; for the comic effect is almost unavoidable when the thought is awakened of a girl's seven fruitless attempts to be married, even though she was quite close to it — as close as a student who has been failed seven times for the *Attestats*. In the Book of Tobit the accent lies elsewhere, and therefore the high number is of importance, and in a certain sense even tragically contributing; for so much the greater is the young Tobias's magnanimity, partly insofar as he is his parents' only son (6:15), partly because the deterrent more pressingly impinges. This must, then, be put aside. Sarah is then a girl who has never loved, who still carries within herself a young girl's blessedness, her enormous priority bond on existence, her *Vollmachtbrief zum Glücke* — to love a man with her whole heart. And yet she is more unhappy than anyone, for she knows that the evil demon who loves her will kill the bridegroom on the wedding night. I have read of much sorrow, but I doubt whether anywhere there is to be found such a deep sorrow as that which lies in this girl's life. When a misfortune comes from outside, then there is consolation to be found. Even if existence did not bring a person what could have made him happy, it is still a consolation that he could have received it. But the unfathomable sorrow which no time can disperse, no time heal — to know that it was no help, even if existence did everything! A Greek author hides in his simple naïveté so infinitely much when he says: *πάντως γὰρ οὐδεὶς Ἔρωτα ἔφυγεν ἢ φεύξεται, μέχρι ἂν κάλλος ᾖ καὶ ὀφθαλμοὶ βλέπωσιν* (cf. Longus, *Pastoralia*). There has been many a girl who became unhappy in love; but she did become so; Sarah was so before she became so. It is heavy not to find the one to whom one can give oneself, but it is unspeakably heavy not to be able to give oneself. A young girl gives herself, and then it is said: now she is no longer free; but Sarah was never free, and yet she had never given herself. It is heavy if a girl gave herself and was deceived; but Sarah was deceived before she gave herself. What sorrow of the world lies in what follows, when Tobias finally wishes to marry her! What wedding ceremonies, what preparations! No girl has been deceived as Sarah was; for she was deceived of the most blessed thing of all, the absolute wealth which even the poorest girl owns; deceived of the secure, unbounded, unbridled, unrestrained abandonment of self-giving. For first there was to be smoke, when the heart of the fish and the liver were laid on the glowing embers. And how must the mother not take leave of the daughter, who, like herself deceived of everything, must, in continuity with this, deceive the mother of the most beautiful thing? One only need read the story. Edna prepared the chamber and led Sarah into it, and wept, and received her daughter's tears. And she said to her: my child, be of good cheer! May the Lord of heaven and earth give you joy for this your sorrow! Daughter, be of good cheer. And now the wedding moment — let one read it, if one can for tears: but when they were both shut up together, Tobias rose up from the bed and said:
Stand up, sister! and let us pray, that the Lord may have mercy on us (8:4).

If a poet read this story, if he would use it, I would bet a hundred to one that he would lay everything on the young Tobias. The heroism of being willing to risk his life in such an evident danger — about which the story reminds us once more, for Raguel says the morning after the wedding to Edna: send one of the maidservants and let her see whether he is alive; but if not, that I may bury him, and no one shall know it (cf. 8:13) — this heroism would become the task. I take the liberty of proposing another. It is bold and brave and chivalrous of Tobias to act so; but every man who has not the courage for it is a sissy who knows neither what love is, nor what it is to be a man, nor what is worth living for; he has not even grasped the little mystery, that it is better to give than to receive, and has no inkling of the great mystery: that it is far harder to receive than to give — that is to say, when one has had courage to do without, and in the time of need was not cowardly. No, Sarah is the heroine. Her I will draw near to, as I have never drawn near to any girl, nor felt myself tempted in thought to draw near to any I have read about. For what love of God is required, in order to want to let oneself be healed when one is in this way from the beginning unhinged through no fault of one's own — from the beginning a botched specimen of a human being! What ethical maturity to take upon oneself the responsibility of permitting the beloved such a daring venture! What humility before another person! What faith in God, that she should not in the next moment hate the man to whom she owed everything!
Let Sarah be a man, and the demonic lies right at hand. The proud, noble nature can endure everything; but one thing it cannot endure — it cannot endure

compassion. There lies a wrong in it, which can only be inflicted on him by a higher power; for by himself he can never become its object. If he has sinned, he can bear the punishment without despairing; but to be without guilt singled out from his mother's womb as the object of compassion, a sweet smell in its nostrils — this he cannot endure. Compassion has a strange dialectic; in one moment it demands guilt, in the next it will not have it; and therefore being predestined to compassion becomes more and more dreadful, the more the individual's misfortune is in the direction of the spiritual. But Sarah has no guilt; she is thrown out as prey to all sufferings, and on top of that she must be tortured by people's compassion; for even I, who admire her more than Tobias loved her, even I cannot mention her name without saying: poor girl. Let a man be in Sarah's place; let him know that, if he will love a girl, then a hellish spirit will come and murder the beloved on the wedding night — then it is well possible that he chose the demonic; he closed himself up in himself, and said in the way a demonic nature speaks in secret: ‘Thank you, I am no friend of ceremonies and elaborateness; I do not at all desire the joy of love; I might as well become a Bluebeard, who has his delight in seeing girls sink down on the wedding night.' One generally learns very little about the demonic, although this region precisely in our age has a valid claim to be discovered, although the observer, when he otherwise knows how to set himself in a little rapport with the demon, can almost use any person at least momentarily. Shakespeare is and always remains, in this direction, a hero. That dreadful demon, the most demonic figure Shakespeare has portrayed, but also portrayed matchlessly — Gloucester (afterward Richard the Third) — what made him a demon? Plainly this: that he could not bear compassion, to which from childhood he had been given over. His monologue in the first act of *Richard the Third* is worth more than entire moral systems, which have no inkling of the terrors of existence, or of the explanation.

*Ich, roh geprägt, und aller Reize baar / Vor leicht sich dreh'nden Nymphen mich zu brüsten; / Ich, so verkürzt um schönes Ebenmass, / Geschändet von der tückischen Natur, / Entstellt, verwahrlost, vor der Zeit gesandt / In diese Welt des Athmens, halb kaum fertig / Gemacht, und zwar so lahm und ungeziemend, / Dass Hunde bellen, hink' ich wo vorbei.*

Such natures as Gloucester's one cannot save by mediating them into an idea of society. Ethics really only mocks them — as it would be a mockery of Sarah if it were to say to her: why do you not express the universal and get married? Such natures are from the bottom of their being in the paradox; and they are by no means more imperfect than other people, only that they are either lost in the demonic paradox or saved in the divine. People have, on and off, taken pleasure in the fact that witches, gnomes, trolls, and the like were misshapen creatures; and it cannot be denied that every person has a tendency, when he sees a misshapen person, at once to attach to it the conception of a moral depravity. What an enormous injustice — since the relationship must rather be inverted: existence itself has corrupted them, as a stepmother makes the children unruly. Originally, by nature or historical condition, to be set outside the universal — that is the beginning of the demonic, of which the individual is not himself guilty. Cumberland's *The Jew* is in this way also a demon, even if he does what is good. So the demonic can also express itself as contempt for people — a contempt which, mark well, does not bring the demonic person himself to act contemptibly; on the contrary, he has his strength in knowing that he is better than all who judge him. — Concerning all such things the poet ought first and foremost to raise an alarm. God knows what writings the now-living younger versifiers read! Their study probably consists in learning rhymes by heart. God knows what their significance in existence is! At this moment I do not know that they are of any other use than that they furnish an edifying proof of the soul's immortality, since one can confidently say of them to oneself what Baggesen says of the city's poet Kildevalle: if he becomes immortal, then we all become so. — What has been said here in connection with Sarah, mainly in the direction of poetic production, and therefore with a fantastic presupposition, has its full meaning when one would, with psychological interest, sink into the meaning of the old saying: *nullum unquam exstitit magnum ingenium sine aliqua dementia*. For this *dementia* is the genius's suffering in existence — is the expression for, if I dare put it so, the divine envy, while the genial is the expression of preferential love. Thus the genius is from the beginning disoriented in relation to the universal, and brought into relation to the paradox — whether, in despair over his limitation, which in his eyes transforms his omnipotence into impotence, he seeks a demonic appeasement and therefore will not acknowledge it either before God or before people, or whether he religiously calms himself in love for the deity. Here lie psychological tasks on which, it seems to me, one might gladly sacrifice an entire life; and yet so seldom does one hear a word about them. In what relation does mental derangement stand to genius? Can one construct the one out of the other? In what sense and to what extent is the genius master over his derangement? For it follows of itself that he, to a certain degree, is master over it, since otherwise he really would be deranged. To such observations, however, belong shrewdness in a high degree and love; for to observe the superior is most difficult. If with attention to this one would read through some of the most genial authors, then it might still be possible, just very seldom and even with much trouble, to discover a little.

One more case I will think of, that a single individual by being hidden and by his silence wishes to save the universal. For this I can use the legend of Faust. Faust is a doubter, a spirit's apostate, who walks the way of the flesh.

This is the poets' view; and although it is repeated again and again that every age has its Faust, still one of its poets after another walks unwearied along the well-trodden highway. Let us undertake a small alteration. Faust is the doubter *kat' exochen*; but he is a sympathetic nature. Even in Goethe's interpretation of Faust, I miss a deeper psychological insight into the secret conversations of doubt with itself. In our age, when after all everyone has experienced doubt, no poet has yet taken a step in this direction. I think therefore I might safely offer them royal stationery to write on, in order to write down all the much they in this respect have experienced — they would scarcely write more than would fit on the very front margin.

Only when one in this way bends Faust into himself, only then can doubt take itself out poetically, only then does he properly discover, in actuality, all its sufferings. He knows then that it is spirit that bears existence, but he also knows that the security and joy in which people live are not grounded in the power of spirit, but easily explainable as unreflected blissfulness. As doubter, as the doubter, he is higher than all this; and if anyone would deceive him by making him believe that he had passed through doubt, he easily sees through it; for he who has made a movement in the world of spirit — that is, an infinite movement — he can immediately

existence. I demand, then, this magnanimity of him; but if he has it, dare he then be silent? Ethics is a dangerous science; and it would well be possible that Aristophanes, determined purely ethically, has resolved to let laughter pass judgment on the deluded age. Aesthetic magnanimity cannot help, for on that score one does not venture such a thing. If he is to be silent, then he must enter into the paradox. — One more sketch I will indicate: that, for example, a person possesses an explanation of a hero's life, which in a sad way explains it, and yet a whole age rests absolutely securely in this hero, without suspecting any such thing.

hear through the line, whether it is a tested man speaking, or a Munchausen. What a Tamerlane can do with his Huns, that Faust knows he can do with his doubt — to startle people up in horror, to let existence sway under their feet, to splinter people apart, to make the cry of anxiety sound everywhere. And if he does it, then he is, after all, no Tamerlane; he is in a certain sense authorized, and has the authorization of thought. But Faust is a sympathetic nature; he loves existence; his soul knows no envy; he sees that he cannot stop the raging he can well awaken; he covets no Herostratic glory — he is silent; he hides the doubt in his soul more carefully than the girl who hides the fruit of a sinful love beneath her heart; he tries as well as he can to keep step with other people; but what goes on in him he consumes within himself, and so he brings himself as a sacrifice for the universal.

One can sometimes hear people lament when an eccentric head sets the whirl of doubt going; they then say: would that he had been silent! This idea Faust realizes. He who has any conception of what it means that a person lives by spirit also knows what the hunger of doubt means, and that the doubter hungers just as much for daily bread as for spiritual nourishment. Even though, then, all the pain Faust suffers can be a quite good argument that it is not pride that has possessed him, still I will use a small precaution which I easily devise; for as Gregory of Rimini was called *tortor infantium*, because he assumed the damnation of small children, so I might be tempted to call myself *tortor heroum*, for I am very inventive when it comes to torturing the heroes. Faust sees Margaret — not after he has chosen lust, for my Faust does not choose lust at all; he sees Margaret not in Mephistopheles' concave mirror, but in all her lovely innocence; and since his soul has preserved love for people, he can also very well fall in love with her. But he is a doubter; his doubt has annihilated actuality for him; for so ideal is my Faust that he does not belong to those scientific doubters who doubt for one hour each semester at the lectern, but otherwise can do everything else, just as they do this — without the condition of spirit, or by virtue of spirit. He is a doubter, and the doubter hungers just as much for joy's daily bread as for spirit's food. Yet he remains true to his resolve and is silent, and speaks to no person about his doubt, and to Margaret either of his love.

It follows of itself that Faust is too ideal a figure to put up with the chatter that, if he spoke, he would occasion a general discussion, or the whole thing would pass off without consequence, or perhaps, or perhaps. (Here slumbers, as every poet will easily see, the comic in the sketch — by bringing Faust into an ironic relation to those low-comic fools who in our age run after doubt, who put forth an outward argument that they really have doubted — for example, a doctor's certificate — or swear that they have doubted everything, or prove it by the fact that on their journey they fell in with a doubter; these expresses and quick-runners in the world of spirit, who in great haste pick up at one person a little inkling of doubt, at another of faith, and now *wirthschaften* in the best way, just as the parish wants fine sand or coarse.) Faust is too ideal a figure to walk in train. He who has not an infinite passion is not ideal, and he who has an infinite passion has long since saved his soul out of such drivel. He is silent in order to sacrifice himself — or he speaks with the consciousness that he will confuse everything.
If he is silent, then ethics passes judgment on him; for it says:

‘You shall acknowledge the universal, and you acknowledge it precisely by speaking, and you dare not have compassion on the universal.' This consideration one ought not to forget when one occasionally judges a doubter strictly because he speaks. I am not inclined to judge such conduct mildly; but here, as everywhere, it depends on the movements being made normally. If wrong is to be done, then a doubter — even if by speaking he brought all possible misfortune upon the world — is far to be preferred to those wretched sweet-tooths who taste everything, and who would cure doubt without knowing it, and who therefore generally are the proximate occasion for doubt's breaking forth wildly and ungovernably. — If he speaks, then he confuses everything; for whether or not it happens, he learns only afterward, and the outcome cannot help one — neither in the moment of action, nor with respect to responsibility.

If he is silent on his own responsibility, then he can indeed act magnanimously; but to his other pain he will feel a small temptation; for the universal will constantly torment him and say: you should have spoken; where will you find the certainty that it was not, after all, a hidden pride that governed your decision?

If, on the other hand, the doubter can become the single individual who as the single individual stands in an absolute relation to the absolute, then he can get an authorization for his silence. In that case he must make his doubt into guilt. In that case he is in the paradox; but in that case his doubt is healed, even if he might get another doubt.

Even the New Testament would acknowledge such a silence. There even occur passages in the New Testament that praise irony, only that it is used to hide the better. This movement, however, is just as much that of irony as of anything else that has its ground in the fact that subjectivity is higher than actuality. This our age will know nothing of; it will, in general, know nothing more about irony than what Hegel has said, who, oddly enough, did not understand much about it, and bore a grudge against it, which our age has good reason not to give up; for it must merely beware of irony. It is said in the Sermon on the Mount: when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, that people may not see that you are fasting. This passage testifies plainly that subjectivity is incommensurable with actuality, indeed that it has the right to deceive. If only those people who in our age go feeling around with loose talk about the idea of the congregation would read the New Testament, then they might perhaps come to other thoughts.

But now Abraham — how did he act? For I have not forgotten, and the reader will now perhaps be pleased to remember, that it was in order to come up against this that I let myself in for the whole foregoing investigation — not as if Abraham would by it become more intelligible, but in order that the unintelligibility might become more desultory; for, as I said, Abraham I cannot understand, him I can only admire. It was also remarked that none of the stages described contained an analogy to Abraham; they were only developed so that, while they were shown within their own sphere, they might in the moment of misalignment, as it were, indicate the boundary of the unknown land. Insofar as there should be any question of an analogy, it would have to be the paradox of sin; but this lies again in another sphere, and cannot explain Abraham, and is itself far more easily explained than Abraham.
Abraham, then, did not speak; he did not speak to Sarah, not to Eliezer, not to Isaac; he passed by the three ethical instances. For the ethical had for Abraham no higher expression than family life.
Aesthetics permitted — yes, demanded — silence of the single individual when by his silence he could save another.

This already shows sufficiently that Abraham does not lie within the compass of aesthetics. His silence is by no means in order to save Isaac; just as, in general, his whole task — to sacrifice Isaac for his own and for God's sake — is an offense to aesthetics; for aesthetics can well understand that I sacrifice myself, but not that I sacrifice another for my own sake. The aesthetic hero was silent. Ethics, however, judged him because he was silent by virtue of his accidental singularity. It was his human foreknowledge that determined him to be silent. This ethics cannot forgive; every such human knowledge is only an illusion; ethics demands an infinite movement; it demands disclosure. The aesthetic hero, then, can speak, but will not.

The real tragic hero sacrifices himself and all that is his for the universal; his deed, every emotion in him, belongs to the universal; he is manifest, and in this disclosure ethics' beloved son. This does not fit Abraham; he does nothing for the universal, and he is hidden.

Now, then, we stand at the paradox. Either the single individual as the single individual can stand in an absolute relation to the absolute, and then the ethical is not the highest; or else Abraham is lost: he is neither a tragic hero nor an aesthetic hero.

To this extent it can again seem here that the paradox is the easiest and most convenient of all. Meanwhile I must repeat that the one who holds himself convinced of this is not a knight of faith; for need and anxiety are the only justification that can be conceived, even if it cannot be conceived universally — for then the paradox is annulled.

Abraham is silent — but he cannot speak; therein lie the need and the anxiety. For when, as I am speaking, I cannot make myself understandable, then I am not speaking, even if I went on speaking uninterruptedly night and day. This is Abraham's case. He can say everything; but one thing he cannot say; and yet, when he cannot say it — i.e., say it in such a way that another understands it — then he is not speaking. The relieving thing about speech is that it translates me into the universal. Now Abraham can say the most beautiful things any language can produce about how he loves Isaac. But this is not what lies on his mind; it is the deeper thing — that he wants to sacrifice him because it is a trial. This last no one can understand, and so anyone can only misunderstand the first. This need the tragic hero does not know. He has, in the first place, the consolation that every counter-argument has had its due — that he has been able to give Clytemnestra, Iphigenia, Achilles, the chorus, every living being, every voice from the heart of mankind, every cunning, every anxious, every accusing, every compassionate thought the chance to rise up against him. He can be sure that everything that could be said against him has been said, mercilessly, pitilessly — and to fight against the whole world is a consolation; to fight with oneself is dreadful — he need not fear that he has overlooked anything; that one day afterwards he must perhaps cry out as did King Edward IV at the news of Clarence's murder:
*Wer bat für ihn? Wer kniet' in meinem Grimm / Zu Füssen mir und bat mich überlegen? / Wer sprach von Bruderpflicht? Wer sprach von Liebe?*

The tragic hero does not know the dreadful responsibility of solitude. Next, he has the consolation that he can weep and lament with Clytemnestra and Iphigenia — and tears and cries assuage, but unutterable sighs torture. Agamemnon can quickly gather his soul into the certainty that he will act, and then he still has time to console and to encourage. This Abraham cannot do. When his heart is moved, when his words would contain a blessed comfort for the whole world, he dare not console; for would not Sarah, would not Eliezer, would not Isaac say to him: ‘Why then would you do it? you can leave it undone.' And if then in his need he wanted to give vent to his feelings, wanted to embrace everything that was dear to him before he proceeded to the last, then he might bring about the dreadful thing that Sarah, that Eliezer, that Isaac were offended at him and thought him a hypocrite. Speak he cannot; he speaks no human language. Even if he himself understood all the tongues of earth, even if the beloved understood them too, he still cannot speak — he speaks in a divine tongue, he speaks in tongues.

This need I can well understand; I can admire Abraham; I do not fear that anyone, by reason of this story, will be tempted frivolously to want to be the single individual; but I confess too that I do not have the courage for it, and that I gladly renounce every prospect of going further, if only it were possible that I should ever, however late, get so far. At every moment Abraham can break off; he can repent the whole thing as a temptation; then he can speak; then everyone can understand him — but then he is no longer Abraham.

Abraham cannot speak; for he cannot say (i.e., so that it is intelligible) that which would explain everything: that it is a trial — and, mark well, such a one in which the ethical is the temptation. He who is so placed is an emigrant from the sphere of the universal. But the next thing he can still less say. For Abraham makes, as has earlier been sufficiently developed, two movements. He makes the infinite movement of resignation and gives up Isaac — this no one can understand, because it is a private undertaking. But next he makes at every moment faith's
movement. This is his consolation. For he says, i.e.:

yet it will not happen, or if it happens, then the Lord will give me a new Isaac — by virtue, that is, of the absurd. The tragic hero, after all, gets to the end of the story. Iphigenia bows under her father's resolve; she herself makes the infinite movement of resignation, and they are now in understanding with each other. She can understand Agamemnon, because his enterprise expresses the universal. If Agamemnon were, on the other hand, to say to her: ‘Even though the god demands you as a sacrifice, it is still possible that he does not demand it — by virtue, that is, of the absurd' — then he would in the same moment become unintelligible to Iphigenia. If he could say it by virtue of human calculation, then Iphigenia would surely understand him; but then it would follow that Agamemnon had not made the infinite movement of resignation, and then he is not a hero — then the seer's saying is a piece of skipper's gossip, and the whole event is a vaudeville.

Abraham, then, did not speak. Only one word of his is preserved — the only line he says to Isaac, which also sufficiently proves that he had not spoken before. Isaac asks Abraham where the lamb for the burnt offering is. ‘And Abraham said: God will see to the lamb for the burnt offering, my son!'

This last word of Abraham I will here consider a little more closely. Were this word not, then the whole event would be lacking something; were it otherwise, then everything would perhaps dissolve into confusion.

It has often been the object of my deliberation how far a tragic hero, whether he culminates in a suffering or in an action, ought to have a final word. It depends, as far as I can judge, on the sphere of life to which he belongs, on how far his life has intellectual significance, on how far his suffering or action stands in relation to spirit.
It follows of itself that the tragic hero in his

culminating moment, like every other person who has not been deprived of speech, can say a few words, perhaps a few fitting words; but the question is how far it is fitting for him to say them. If the meaning of his life lies in an outward deed, then he has nothing to say; then everything he says is essentially chatter, by which he only weakens the impression of himself, while the tragic ceremonial commands that he silently fulfill his task — whether this consists in a deed or a suffering. Not to go too far, I will only take what lies most immediately at hand. If Agamemnon himself, not Calchas, were to draw the knife against Iphigenia, then he would only have demeaned himself by, in the last moment, wanting to say a few words; for the meaning of his deed was, after all, evident to all; the procedure of piety, of pity, of feeling, of tears was completed; and besides, his life had no relation to spirit, i.e., he was no teacher or witness of spirit. If, on the other hand, the meaning of a hero's life is in the direction of spirit, then the lack of a line would weaken the impression of him. What he then has to say is not a few fitting words, a little declamation piece, but the meaning of his line is that he carries himself through in the decisive moment. Such an intellectual tragic hero ought to have, and ought to keep, the last word. One demands of him the same transfigured bearing that befits every tragic hero; but then one demands one more word. Insofar, then, as such an intellectual tragic hero culminates in a suffering (in death), then in this last word he becomes immortal before he dies — while, on the contrary, the ordinary tragic hero only becomes immortal after his death. One can use Socrates as an example. He was an intellectual tragic hero. His death sentence is announced to him. In that moment he dies; for he who does not understand that the whole power of the spirit is required to die, and that the hero always dies before he dies, will not get very far in his consideration of life. Now, as a hero, it is required of Socrates that he rest calmly in himself; but as an intellectual tragic hero, it is required of him that in this last moment he have spirit-strength enough to carry himself through. He cannot then, like the ordinary tragic hero, concentrate on holding himself up over against death, but he must so quickly make this movement that in the same moment with his consciousness he is past this struggle and asserts himself. Thus, if Socrates in death's crisis had become silent, he would have weakened the effect of his life, awakened a suspicion that the elasticity of irony in him was not a world-power, but a play whose resilience in the decisive moment would have to be used in inverse measure to hold him up pathetically *.

What has here been briefly hinted at cannot indeed find its application to Abraham, insofar as one means that by some analogy one might be able to find a fitting word for Abraham to end with; but rather insofar as one perceives the necessity that Abraham in the last moment must carry himself through, must not silently draw the knife, but must have a word to say, since as the father of faith he has absolute significance in the direction of spirit. What he is to say, of that I can form no conception in advance; after he has said it, then I can well understand, well in a certain sense understand Abraham in the

Which line of Socrates' is to be regarded as the decisive one — about that opinions can be divided, since Socrates has in so many ways been poetically transfigured by Plato. I propose the following: the death sentence is announced to him; in the same moment he dies; in the same moment he overcomes death and carries himself through in the famous reply: that it surprised him that he had been condemned by a majority of three votes. With no loose and idle talk in the marketplace, with no foolish remark of an idiot, could he have jested more ironically than with that death sentence which condemles him himself from life.

matter, without thereby being any closer to him than I have been to him in the foregoing. If there had existed no last line of Socrates, then I could have thought myself into him and formed such a one; if I could not have done it, a poet could have managed it; but Abraham no poet can reach.

Before I pass over to a closer consideration of Abraham's last words, I must first call attention to the difficulty of Abraham's being able to come to say anything at all. The need and the anxiety in the paradox lay, as developed above, precisely in the silence: Abraham cannot speak *. To this extent it is, then, a self-contradiction to demand that he should speak — unless one wishes to have him out again of the paradox, in such a way that he in the decisive moment suspends it, by which he then ceases to be Abraham and annuls the whole foregoing. Thus, if Abraham now in the decisive moment were to say to Isaac: it is you, the matter concerns — then this would only be a weakness. For if he could speak at all, then he would have had to speak long before, and the weakness would lie in his not having had spirit's maturity and concentration to think through the whole pain in advance, but had pushed something away from himself, so that the actual pain was a *more* than the thought one. Besides, he would by such a speech fall out of the paradox; and if he really wanted to speak with Isaac, he would have to transform his condition into a temptation; for otherwise he could after all say nothing; and if he does this, then he is not even any kind of tragic hero.
Meanwhile a final word of Abraham is, after all, preserved; and insofar as I can understand the paradox, I can

* Insofar as there can be any question of an analogy, Pythagoras's death-situation provides one; for the silence he had always maintained he had to carry through in his last moment, and therefore he said: it is better to be killed than to speak. Cf. Diogenes, Book 8, §39.

also understand Abraham's total presence in this word. He says, first and foremost, nothing; and in this form he says what he has to say. His answer to Isaac has the form of irony, for it is always irony when I say something and yet say nothing. Isaac asks Abraham, in the conviction that Abraham knows. If Abraham now were to have answered: I know nothing — then he would have said an untruth. Say something he cannot, for what he knows he cannot say. He answers, then: God will see to the lamb for the burnt offering, my son! One sees from this the double movement in Abraham's soul, as it has been described in the foregoing. Had Abraham only resigned Isaac and not done more, then he would have said an untruth; for he knows, after all, that God demands Isaac as a sacrifice, and he knows that he himself precisely in this moment is ready to sacrifice him. He has, then, at every moment, after having made this movement, made the next — has made the movement of faith by virtue of the absurd. To this extent he says no untruth; for by virtue of the absurd, it is, after all, possible that God could do something quite different. He says, then, no untruth; but neither does he say anything — for he speaks in a foreign tongue. This becomes still more evident when we consider that it was Abraham himself who was to sacrifice Isaac. Had the task been a different one — had the Lord commanded Abraham to bring Isaac out to Mount Moriah, where the Lord himself would let his lightning strike Isaac and so take him as a sacrifice — then Abraham could in the straightforward sense have been right to speak as enigmatically as he does; for then he himself could not have known what would happen. But as the task is set for Abraham, he is himself to act; he must therefore in the decisive moment know what he himself will do, and so he must know that Isaac is to be sacrificed. If he has not known this with definiteness, then he has not made the infinite movement of resignation; then his word is indeed not an untruth, but he is also very far from being Abraham — he is more insignificant than a tragic hero; indeed, he is an irresolute man, who can decide neither for the one nor for the other, and who on that account will always come to speak in riddles. But such a hesitator is precisely the parody of the knight of faith.

It shows itself again here that one can well understand Abraham, but understand him only in the way one understands the paradox. I, for my part, can well understand Abraham; but I also grasp that I do not have the courage to speak in this way, just as little as I have the courage to act as Abraham did; but by this I by no means say that it is something insignificant, since on the contrary it is the only wondrous thing.

And what did the contemporary age judge of the tragic hero? That he was great, and it admired him. And that venerable assembly of the noble, the jury which every generation constitutes to judge the previous generation — it judged the same. But Abraham there was no one who could understand. And yet what did he attain? That he remained true to his love. But he who loves God needs no tears, no admiration; he forgets the suffering in the love — yes, so completely has he forgotten it, that there should not even afterward be the slightest hint of his pain, if God himself did not remember it; for he sees in secret, and knows the need, and counts the tears, and forgets nothing.
Either, then, there is a paradox: that the single individual as the single individual stands in an absolute relation to the absolute; or else Abraham is lost.

chapters.title: Epilogue
paragraphs: Once, in Holland, when the prices of spices became somewhat sluggish, the merchants had a couple of cargoes sunk in the sea in order to screw up the price. This was a forgivable, perhaps a necessary deception. Is it something similar that we need in the world of spirit? Are we so convinced that we have come to the highest, that there is nothing else left but piously to make ourselves believe that we have not come so far, only in order to find something with which to fill out the time? Is it such a self-deception that the present generation needs? Is it for a virtuosity in this that it is to be educated? Or is it not, rather, sufficiently perfected in the art of deceiving itself? Or is what it needs not, rather, an honest seriousness which fearlessly and incorruptibly points to the tasks — an honest seriousness which lovingly safeguards the tasks, which does not frighten people into trying to startle themselves into the highest, but keeps the tasks young and beautiful and lovely to look at, and beckoning to all, and yet difficult and inspiring for the noble — for the noble nature is inspired only by what is difficult? Whatever one generation may learn from another, the properly human no generation learns from a previous one.

In this respect every generation begins primitively, has no other task than every previous generation, comes no further either, insofar as the previous generation did not betray the task and deceive itself. This properly human is passion, in which also one generation perfectly understands another and understands itself. So no generation has learned to love from another; no generation comes to begin at any other point than at the beginning; no later generation has a shorter task than the previous one; and if here one will not, like the previous generations, stop at loving, but go further — then this is only an idle and foolish talk.

But the highest passion in a human being is faith, and no generation begins here at any other point than the previous one; every generation begins from the beginning; the following generation does not get further than the previous one, insofar as that one was true to its task and did not leave it in the lurch. That this should be wearying is, of course, something the generation cannot say; for the generation, after all, has the task, and has nothing to do with the fact that the previous generation had the same task — unless the individual generation, or the individuals in the generation, presumptuously want to take the place which belongs only to the spirit that governs the world, and which has patience not to grow weary. If the generation begins on such a thing, then it is upside down; and what wonder, then, that the whole of existence seems to it upside down? For surely no one has found existence more upside down than the tailor who, according to the fairy tale, came up to heaven alive and from this standpoint regarded the world. As soon as the generation only concerns itself with its task, which is the highest, then it cannot become wearied; for the task is always sufficient for a human life. When children on a holiday have, before twelve o'clock, already played through all their games, and now impatiently say: Is there no one then who can think up a new game? — does this prove that these children are more developed and more advanced than the children in their own time or in a past generation, who could let the familiar games suffice for the whole day? Or does it not rather prove that those first children lack what I would call the lovely seriousness that belongs to play?

Faith is the highest passion in a human being. There are perhaps, in every generation, many who do not even come to it, but no one comes further. Whether also in our age there are many who do not discover it, I do not decide; I dare appeal only to myself, who do not conceal that he has long prospects ahead of him, without therefore wishing to deceive himself or the great by making this into an insignificance, into a childhood disease that one must wish to be over with as soon as possible. But also for the one who does not even come to faith, life has tasks enough, and if he loves these honestly, then his life shall not be wasted either, even if it is never like the lives of those who sensed and grasped the highest. But the one who came to faith (whether he be the eminently gifted or the simple — that makes no difference to the case), he does not stop at faith; indeed, he would be offended if anyone said it to him, just as the lover would be indignant if one said that he stopped at love; for, he would answer, by no means do I stop, since I have my life in it. Yet he does not get further either, not to anything else; for when he discovers this, then he has another explanation.

‘One must go further; one must go further.' This urge to go further is old in the world. The dark Heraclitus, who deposited his thoughts in his writings and his writings in the temple of Diana (for his thoughts had been his armor in life, and therefore he hung it up in the temple of the god) — the dark Heraclitus said: one cannot go twice through the same

river *. The dark Heraclitus had a disciple; he did not stop here, he went further, and added: one cannot do it even once **. Poor Heraclitus, to have such a disciple! By this improvement the Heraclitean proposition was improved into an Eleatic proposition, which denies motion; and yet that disciple wished only to be a disciple of Heraclitus, who went further — not back to that which Heraclitus had left.
